#126392. Latest Update: GPTBot is blocked on 17.7% of sites. PerplexityBot on 15.2%. Which AI engines can actually read you?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (678 w)

Latest Update: GPTBot is blocked on 17.7% of sites. PerplexityBot on 15.2%. Which AI engines can actually read you?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most AI visibility advice treats "AI crawlers" as a single category.
  • I sent live HTTP requests to 513 reachable sites, each time as a different AI crawler user agent.
  • GPTBot is the most blocked crawler by a margin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most AI visibility advice treats "AI crawlers" as a single category. They are not. Each crawler has a different blocking rate, a different purpose, and a different relationship to the engine that cites your content. I tested six of them across 513 sites. The numbers are different enough that treating them as one group hides the real picture.

I sent live HTTP requests to 513 reachable sites, each time as a different AI crawler user agent. Here is what came back:.

GPTBot is the most blocked crawler by a margin. It is also the most talked about. Articles about "blocking ChatGPT from scraping your site" almost always refer to GPTBot, and the data highlights site owners are acting on that advice.

These six bots serve three different purposes, and blocking them has different consequences:.

Sources indicate that training crawlers. GPTBot and Googlebot (when configured as Google-Extended) collect data for model training. Blocking them means your content will not influence future model versions. This is a legitimate choice for publishers who want to keep content out of training data.

Citation crawlers. OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, and Claude-SearchBot fetch pages in real time to generate citations in AI search results. Blocking them means AI engines cannot read your page when a user asks a question. You disappear from AI answers. This is almost never intentional.

Discovery crawlers. Applebot feeds Apple Intelligence and Spotlight. Googlebot feeds traditional Google search and AI Overviews. Blocking Googlebot is catastrophic for regular SEO. 64 sites in the sample block it, 49 of them as part of a blanket block on all non-browser user agents.

GPTBot is a training crawler. OAI-SearchBot is a citation crawler. Both are from OpenAI. Many site owners block GPTBot to keep content out of training data, which is a valid choice. But they do not add an Allow rule for OAI-SearchBot. The result: they block training AND citations from ChatGPT, when they only meant to block training.

Sources indicate that in the sample, 65 sites block both GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot. Zero sites block GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot while allowing PerplexityBot. This means the 65 sites that block the OpenAI pair are blocking all OpenAI citation traffic. If you want to block training but keep citations, the robots.txt is:.

It has been revealed that this tells GPTBot to stay out and OAI-SearchBot to come in. The default for OAI-SearchBot, if not listed, depends on the wildcard rule. Many sites have User-agent: * Disallow: / which blocks everything not explicitly allowed. That is why OAI-SearchBot needs an explicit Allow.

Industry observers note that 45 sites block specific AI bots while letting the browser through. The patterns:.

This number should alarm anyone who cares about regular SEO. 64 sites out of 513 block Googlebot. 49 of those are blanket blocks (all bots including browser). 15 block Googlebot while the browser passes.

A blanket block is bad but at least consistent: the site owner knows something is wrong because their SEO traffic drops. The 15 sites that block Googlebot while allowing browsers are the dangerous case. The site works in Chrome. Google Analytics demonstrates traffic. But Googlebot gets a 403. The site is slowly disappearing from search results and nobody notices until the traffic drops weeks later.

If you use a CDN or a security plugin, test Googlebot access. curl -A "Googlebot/2.1" -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://yoursite.com. If you get 403, fix it before it costs you organic traffic.

According to recent reports, the takeaway is that "is my site visible to AI?" is six separate questions, not one. A robots.txt check for GPTBot does not tell you whether OAI-SearchBot can reach you. A Cloudflare check for GPTBot does not tell you whether PerplexityBot passes.

It has been revealed that if you want the full check, run a free audit on geoready.dev. The audit tests 27 AI crawlers at the robots.txt level and sends live HTTP requests as the four most crucial citation bots.

The CLI is on GitHub, MIT licensed. pip install geo-optimizer && geo audit https://yoursite.com.

17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science highlights that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.
  • We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year.
  • Recent findings suggest that laura M.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that joy! What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science highlights that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.

We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year. The responses did not disappoint! Here are a few that span ages, time commitments, and subject areas.

Recent findings suggest that laura M. (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment. Providing time for activities like dancing is often seen as an “extra.” Building this activity into our weekly schedule has become a favorite stress-relieving activity—adding tremendous joy and connection between children and children and children and teachers.

Related Greater Good in Education (GGiE) practices: The World Is a Dance; Getting to Know Each Other Through Dance; We Are Better Dancing Together.

Josh (Latest Haven, CT): Every Monday morning meeting, students greet each other by asking, “What brought you joy (made you smile/laugh) over the weekend?”.

Laura H.: At the end of the day, with second graders, we share the activity from our day that brought the most joy. If I wasn’t there for it (i.e., recess, music, art, PE), I ask them to include details.

Related GGiE practices: Noticing Kindness; Giving Thanks; Looking for Gratitude in School; Sharing Gratitude Stories.

Emi (Lobitos, Peru): Identifying forms of enchantment—I use this approach in our Women & Water Program. It’s an all-girls (ages 3–16) surf, science, and storytelling program based in Lobitos, a tiny fishing village in Northern Peru. We use “enchantment” as a way for young girls to foster their curiosity, creativity, and care for themselves, peers, community, and the coastal environment. We do this through photography (taking “macro” photos of small, wondrous things found in their environment, like a flower petal, a beetle, etc.). Or we do this in surfing—the girls notice the “awe” of riding the energy of a leftover storm until it crashes into the sand. These girls also made this song after an oil spill that rocked our community about two years ago.

Related GGiE practices: Meaningful Photos for Students; Mindfully Finding Awe in Nature.

Angela (Pleasant Hill, CA): I am a school counselor and with my students who experience anxiety we use sidewalk chalk to write positive welcoming messages and pictures in front of our school. It makes others feel welcomed and helps my students feel connected to our school. They even told me it helps get them to school the first couple of days knowing they would see their chalk messages.

Related GGiE practices: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness; Kindness Buddy; Awe-Inspiring Affirmations.

According to recent reports, lorien (St. Louis, MO): Have a “Would you rather…?” question on the whiteboard at the start of class—the funnier the better. Students put a checkmark next to their choice. It’s a fun way to welcome the “whole student self” into the classroom, not just their “learner selves.” Sometimes we talk about it, but often, we don’t.

Related GGiE practice: Superstar.

In a recent development, pam (Muscogee County, GA): To kick off the year, my eighth graders design and build a cardboard maze that guides three different rolling spheres from start to finish. Working in teams of four, students sketch a plan, build it with cardboard and hot glue, test it, and revise their design. Nothing works perfectly the first time. Students quickly discover that failure is a useful part of the design process. By the end of the week, teams are cheering when a ping pong ball, golf ball, or rubber ball finally makes it all the way through, and that joy comes from earning it through real trial and error. It sets the tone for the whole year: Engineering is a process of building, testing, and improving.

Kimberly (Williamsport, PA): Something that I introduce during the first week of classes is our 3 Good Things or 3 Little Wins Padlet. Each week students post about three good things or little wins they had during the week. Before the first post, we discuss why it is notable to celebrate these things, no matter how small (e.g., a good cup of coffee!). We also discuss the impact that reflecting on these things has on our physical and psychological well-being. Each week I also post my wins for the week and comment on student posts as well. It creates a wonderful community!

Related GGIE practices: Three Good Things for Students; Gratitude Journals.

Jonah (Duxbury, VT): As a high school English teacher, the first writing assignment I give to students asks them to choose a (clean) song that represents them and tell me why they feel connected to this song. I then make a playlist including all the students’ songs, and play it during work times or use it to play students’ walk-up song on special days like birthdays.

Related GGiE practices: Creating Musical Playlists for the Classroom; Prosocial Music Hub (13 practices to bring music into the classroom).

Industry observers note that joe (Bridgeport, CT): Students interact with each other as they navigate around the crowded classroom, connected only by cake-pop sticks balanced between each other using only their index finger. Fosters concentration, cooperation, joyful failures, interconnectedness, and intimacy without actually touching one another.

Related GGiE practice: 1-2-3 Clap.

David (San Antonio, TX): For my introductory geology class, I work with the students to develop rules for a “rock-rock-rock” (igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic) version of “rock-paper-scissors.” Students develop the necessary hand signals and the action verbs that say what beats what. Once we have the rules established, the students engage in a best two out of three to crown the class champion. Branded university swag is available for the winners, and everyone gets a candy treat for participating.

Related GGiE practice: Making Science Meaningful.

Susan (St. Paul, MN): I ask students to tell the rest of the class their name and a ridiculous lie about themselves—the more absurd the better. There’s always good-natured laughter and encouragement.

Related GGiE practice: Truth or Tale.

Harry (Hailey, ID): I work to end every “session” (class, administration meeting, faculty meeting, etc.) with laughter, whether incited by me or coming from someone else. That moment becomes the punctuation.

Related GGiE practices: Share a Laugh; The SEL 3 Signature Practices.

Paige (Seattle, WA): About the second or third week of classes (graduate and undergraduate students) we begin doing this ritual that we do a few times during the semester: “The joy of contribution…I see this in you!” Students take turns identifying something they have genuinely observed in another student in the cohort/class: “One leadership capacity I see developing in you is________, because I watched you ________.” The BECAUSE matters.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Examples I have heard from pre-certified teachers and principals: “I see courage building in you because I have watched you ask questions the rest of us were afraid to ask.” OR, “I see you really owning belongingness as you consistently notice who is outside the conversation and what is happening around us as you read the room.”.

Sources indicate that related GGiE practices: I See You. Everyone Matters; Behind Your Back.

In a recent development, lorien (St. Louis, MO): I use a guided visualization to prompt students to think about what joyful teaching, joyful learning, and joyful interactions look like, sound like, and feel like. It makes what we’re doing much more explicit, and it helps me know what they want from me and vice versa.

Related GGiE practice: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness.

Angela (McMinnville, OR): A non-dominant hand drawing activity that gets us all out of our “perfection” thinking and into being learners…and laughing.

Related GGiE practice: Drawing as a Way to Manage Emotions.

Milton (San Diego, CA): As the associate principal, I stand out in front of the school in the morning with a SUBSTANTIAL SMILE sign on and greet the students with a “Good morning & have a great day!” Some students like a fist bump or handshake as well.

Related GGiE practice: Making Families Feel Welcome.

According to recent reports, donna (Arkansas): “JOY” is the grounding rhythm that closes every day, honoring the joyful moments that JUST happened, recognizing community attunement through something an OTHER person did, and celebrating internal self-efficacy via something YOU did. Each person is free to select whichever letter resonates with them to share. We pass a rainstick around the circle; once it is turned to let its gentle cascade settle into silence, the person holding it speaks. This tactile ritual and quiet sound not only brings a profound sense of calm to the transition from classroom to home, but it also serves as a gentle reminder to carry those reflections outward.

Related GGiE practices: Inspiring Virtue With Moral Beauty; Stories of Moral Beauty; Noticing Kindness; Nurturing Students’ Wonder and Curiosity.

Recent findings suggest that thank you to all of the educators in the Greater Good community who shared activities for bringing joy into schools and classrooms. We received many, many more than we could share here. Even in the face of incredible challenges, you are bringing so much joy to your students and their families, your colleagues, and yourself. May you all have a joyful start to the new school year!

Recent findings suggest that we look forward to our next post in the From Our Readers series that will focus on building community through connection and belonging. Want to share an activity? Fill out this quick form! Not only will you strengthen our community, you’ll be entered into a drawing for a free self-paced course or a spot in our Flourishing Spring community of practice!

According to recent reports, sarah Bracken is the Director of Education Partnerships at Greater Good Science Center. Prior to joining GGSC, Sarah taught in secondary classrooms from Alaska to Virginia and collaborated with educators to co-create communities of practice and other professional learning opportunities focused on belonging and equitable education for students of refugee and immigrant backgrounds. She is a Nationally Board Certified teacher with a B.A. from the University of Virginia and a Master’s in Teaching from The Evergreen State College.

Gemini 4 Neon Arrives With 1M Context, $3 Token Pricing, and Top Coding Agent Scores

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Developers and enterprise teams have spent most of 2026 trading off between heavyweight frontier models that burn budgets and fast, smaller models that stumble on multi-file refactors.
  • Industry observers note that neon brings a 1 million-token context window, four adjustable thinking levels, and aggressive API pricing aimed at high-frequency agentic workflows.
  • Industry observers note that within Google's current family, Gemini 4 Carbon handles the longest, hardest reasoning jobs, while Gemini 4 Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developers and enterprise teams have spent most of 2026 trading off between heavyweight frontier models that burn budgets and fast, smaller models that stumble on multi-file refactors. On November 18, 2026, Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Neon, positioning it directly between the heavy-duty Gemini 4 Carbon and the high-speed Gemini 4 Hydrogen.

Industry observers note that neon brings a 1 million-token context window, four adjustable thinking levels, and aggressive API pricing aimed at high-frequency agentic workflows. It rolled out on launch day across the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, Android Studio, Gemini for business, Google Antigravity for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra owners, and the consumer Gemini app for Pro and Ultra tiers.

Industry observers note that within Google's current family, Gemini 4 Carbon handles the longest, hardest reasoning jobs, while Gemini 4 Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution. Neon targets production coding, analytical research, and complex enterprise tasks where latency and per-task token spend both matter.

Recent findings suggest that API pricing starts at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Cached input tokens drop to $0.15 per million, representing a 95% discount for teams feeding large repositories, PDFs, or knowledge bases repeatedly. According to Google DeepMind's announcement, partner Glean observed Neon matching or exceeding Gemini 4 Carbon on overall quality at three times the speed and 60% of the cost.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, Neon scores 61 and ranks No. 3 overall behind larger, slower models. Even at its default high thinking setting, Google reports a 32% lower cost per task than Gemini 4 Carbon and roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than competing frontier models on the Vals Index and Agent Arena.

Digital chip and neural network illustration representing modern AI model architecture.

Credit: Mike MacKenzie, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Software engineering is where Neon posts its sharpest numbers. It ranks No. 1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6, reaches 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, and scores 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its default high setting.

Scaffold design plays a visible role in multi-file repository work. On SWE-sweep, Neon leads on the mini-SWE runner at 12.8%, then jumps to 39.0% inside Google Antigravity, where it can either run standalone or act as an Orchestrator coordinating parallel Hydrogen subagents.

Recent findings suggest that google also published a set of Antigravity /swarm demonstrations alongside the Gemini 4 Neon model card to show sustained multi-step execution. In one demo, Neon drove Blender MCP to build a 3D lab scene; in another, it generated a WebGL2 ski simulator with 10,200 lines of custom shaders on Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation data; in a third, it converted an image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet using more than 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas with zero Apps Script.

Beyond coding, Neon is built to ingest mixed enterprise inputs inside its 1 million-token window, including spreadsheets, PDFs, dense charts, audio, and video. On Surge AI evaluations, it ranks No. 1 across most finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint-following benchmarks, while scoring 73.5% on Chartography and 75.8% on Agents' Last Exam v1.1.

Long-horizon business and automation tests show similar consistency. Neon ranks No. 1 overall on Zapier's AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), and reaches No. 1 on both Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench. For scientific and mathematical workloads, it posts 70.5% on Terminal-Bench Science, 84.0% on RiemannBench, and 71.3% on HLE-Diamond.

According to recent reports, steerability has become a major pain point for teams using autonomous agents in production, where models often ignore mid-task corrections or burn tokens re-reading files. Neon ranks No. 2 on steerability on the Agent Arena Index and demonstrated a 43% to 56% drop in under-service alongside a 15% to 35% reduction in overreach compared to Carbon's baseline.

Teams building on multimodal or agentic pipelines will recognize how fast pricing and capability tiers are shifting across vendors, from Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash video pricing to Inkling 2 Small open-weight alternatives.

Google DeepMind is also positioning Gemini 4 Neon for defensive security engineering through its Fairwind Program, which begins rolling out to eligible defenders over the coming days. On AutoBaxBench, Neon generates more secure code than Carbon across easy, medium, and hard challenges, reaching 76% on the hard tier.

Across vulnerability discovery, validation, and patching, the published metrics emphasize both accuracy and lower token overhead:.

For enterprise security teams running automated triage across large repositories, lower token consumption directly reduces the operational cost of continuous scanning.

Conceptual illustration of artificial intelligence and machine learning networks.

Credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC0 1.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Recent findings suggest that making a faster, cheaper model frontier-capable raises obvious misuse and reliability questions. Google reports that Neon keeps Carbon-grade safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse while cutting false refusals on legitimate engineering work, refusing 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science.

In a recent development, on agent honesty and shortcut evaluations, Neon recorded 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 2.45% shortcuts on internal coding cheating checks (the lowest in the Gemini 4 family), a 0.09% misaligned action rate, and a 99.2% pass rate on agent honesty tests. When tested against indirect prompt injections hidden inside web pages, emails, documents, or source code on Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon with real-time safeguards at xhigh thinking blocked every attack (0.0% attack success rate).

Developers evaluating Neon via the Gemini API or Google AI Studio can start by testing two specific knobs. First, benchmark your existing prompts at high thinking versus xhigh to see whether high already clears your accuracy bar at lower per-task cost. Second, enable context caching on static repository trees or system instructions to take advantage of the $0.15 per million cached input rate before scaling production traffic.

It has been revealed that choosing between low, medium, high, and xhigh thinking levels determines both latency and monthly API spend for production engineering teams. At $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, Neon sits well below flagship reasoning tiers while keeping a 1 million-token context window available on every request. Teams running large-codebase indexing, compliance audits, or multi-document synthesis gain the biggest savings from prompt caching, where repeated input prefixes drop to $0.15 per million tokens.

When deciding whether to route a workload to Gemini 4 Neon or keep it on Gemini 4 Carbon or Hydrogen, engineering leads can follow a simple split:.

With early rollout access already live across Google AI Studio, Android Studio, and Google Antigravity, teams can benchmark Neon directly against their current production prompts before shifting full traffic.

Industry observers note that engineering teams deploying Gemini 4 Neon in production pipelines get the clearest cost advantage by pairing context caching with structured subagent routing. Static system prompts, repository manifests, architectural docs, and security policy rules fit easily inside the 1 million-token input window and drop to $0.15 per million tokens once cached. In Google Antigravity, using Neon as an Orchestrator to delegate repetitive file searches or unit-test runs to faster Hydrogen workers prevents high-reasoning tokens from being spent on mechanical steps.

At the same time, product teams should verify regional availability and quota limits before flipping production workloads over. Watching early Google AI Developers Forum feedback around Pro tier propagation and running side-by-side accuracy checks on high versus xhigh thinking ensures a smooth migration from older Gemini 3.x or Carbon endpoints.

According to recent reports, teams migrating production agents from Gemini 3.x or Carbon should also track tool-call error rates alongside token spend. Because Neon reduces under-service by 43% to 56% and overreach by 15% to 35% on agentic behavior suites, multi-step pipelines require fewer manual retry loops and recover cleanly from mid-task user corrections, keeping end-to-end latency predictable across long coding, research, and security sessions.

Building a RAG System That States "I Don't Know": Self-Correcting RAG with Llama 3.1 and LangGraph

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (432 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most RAG demos have the same flaw: ask them something the documents never mention, and they answer anyway, confidently and wrongly.
  • I built Llama Agentic RAG around the opposite rule: an answer must be supported by cited sources, or the system notes "I don't know." It runs fully locally on Llama 3.1 8B through Ollama, which fits in 8 GB of VRAM, so private documents never leave the machine.
  • This post walks through the design and the choices that made it work on a small model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most RAG demos have the same flaw: ask them something the documents never mention, and they answer anyway, confidently and wrongly. In a demo that is a curiosity. In production it is how a support bot invents a refund policy.

I built Llama Agentic RAG around the opposite rule: an answer must be supported by cited sources, or the system notes "I don't know." It runs fully locally on Llama 3.1 8B through Ollama, which fits in 8 GB of VRAM, so private documents never leave the machine.

This post walks through the design and the choices that made it work on a small model.

The pipeline is a LangGraph state machine with five stages:.

Industry observers note that the key idea is that hallucinations become refusals, not wrong answers. A refusal is annoying; a confident wrong answer is expensive.

According to recent reports, large models forgive sloppy prompts. Small models don't, so a few details mattered more than any framework choice:.

In a recent development, A RAG system that never notes "I don't know" isn't production-ready, so the evaluation set deliberately includes unanswerable questions. The harness reports:.

Sources indicate that refusal accuracy and false-refusal rate pull against each other, which is exactly why you need both. Tighten the groundedness check and refusals get safer while false refusals rise. The numbers make that trade-off visible instead of a matter of opinion.

Treat prompt and model changes like code changes: they ship only if the evals hold.

Recent findings suggest that CI runs the full graph with scripted fake LLM replies and deterministic embeddings. That covers the happy path, query rewrite, refusal, ungrounded answers, missing citations and reasoning-tag stripping, all without a model or a GPU. It is the cheapest way to keep a graph's control flow honest as it grows.

It has been revealed that the same graph is exposed as an MCP tool, ask_documents, so Claude Desktop, Claude Code or any MCP client can query your documents and get cited answers back. The FastAPI service exposes /ask, /ingest and /health for everything else.

The roadmap is the usual path from reference to production: hybrid retrieval with BM25 and a cross-encoder reranker, a persistent vector database such as pgvector or Qdrant, tracing with Langfuse, streaming, and PDF and DOCX ingestion.

The code is MIT-licensed: github.com/abuzar18/llama-agentic-rag. If you are building RAG for a team that can't afford confident wrong answers, I'd be glad to compare notes.

I'm Abuzar Zulfiqar, an AI/ML engineer who builds production AI agents, RAG assistants and LLM automation. More at abuzar18.github.io.

#126381. How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1329 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.
  • Then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit.
  • Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love the idea of being a runner.

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

Then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

Industry observers note that so I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

Sources indicate that I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

Industry observers note that I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my plan and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

According to recent reports, creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious aims produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

Sources indicate that success is motivating. Doing what you said you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a major part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate prepares but not running.

Sources indicate that small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a plan so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Recent findings suggest that across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

In short: How often beats how long.

I hate the idea of abandoning my massive plans. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

It has been revealed that break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Sources indicate that then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

In a recent development, do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

Sources indicate that expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

At some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this fresh behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

Sources indicate that it’s hard to abandon our grand prepares and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

In a recent development, join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

Industry observers note that christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The New Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.
  • The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.
  • Children and teenagers who report frequent or severe headaches tend to have lower vitamin D levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

Children and teenagers who report frequent or severe headaches tend to have lower vitamin D levels.

The link was modest overall but stronger among girls and among teenagers.

Body mass index, or BMI, accounted for about a fifth of the association in the researchers’ statistical model.

One possibility is that vitamin D and body weight are both related to inflammation, which can affect how sensitive the nervous system is to pain.

Another is that young people who get frequent headaches spend less time outdoors, where sunlight helps the skin produce vitamin D.

The researchers analysed data collected between 2001 and 2004 as part of a US national health and nutrition survey.

The final analysis included just over 5,000 children and teenagers aged six to 19 who had the measurements needed for the study.

The researchers compared blood vitamin D levels with questionnaire reports of frequent or severe headaches, including migraines, in the previous year.

Almost a quarter had experienced headaches that met the survey’s description.

Because the survey grouped several types of headache together, it could not show whether the link was stronger for migraine.

The researchers suggest that inflammation could make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, making mild discomfort feel more intense.

Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

The study was published in the journal Medicine (Zhang et al., 2026).

#126373. Tech Report: Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2258 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time.
  • “We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski states.
  • That changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time. In the 1980s, under Yugoslavia’s “soft” one-party government, Padejski and her friends read Western literature, watched Hollywood movies, and listened to the BBC.

“We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski states.

That changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics. Civil war broke out, and a virulent strain of nationalism took hold in Serbia, the Yugoslavian state where Padejski lived. Firebrand leader Slobodan Milošević ascended to power and began meddling in elections, targeting opposition leaders, and igniting ethnic cleansing campaigns.

Recent findings suggest that “He captured the entire society and his party,” Padejski remembers. “Very soon I found myself on the streets protesting.” Padejski’s activism against repressive Serbian regimes would continue until 2011, when she and her husband, investigative journalist Djordje Padejski, left the country after people threatened to kill them.

Recent findings suggest that the Padejskis arrived in the U.S. with hard-won knowledge of how to outlast repression over the long haul. In recent years, they’ve tapped back into that knowledge and shared it with those around them as they witness here in America the illegal destruction of government agencies, election tampering, and warrantless arrests of citizens and non-citizens. This isn’t just true in the United States—around the world, democracy is declining.

How can we go on defying rising authoritarianism when no clear endpoint is in sight? Psychology and motivation research complement the experience of people like the Padejskis by addressing how to conserve energy and sustain commitment to your ideals in challenging conditions.

“The goal of the authoritarian regime is to desensitize us to extremes, to things we should never agree with or consider normal,” states Djurdja Padejski, now a language and culture researcher (and doctoral candidate) at Arizona State University.

Surviving repression depends on rejecting this presumed “normality” and refusing to let your inner state mirror extremes imposed from above. To that end, here are seven research-backed ways to subsist under indefinite duress.

Recent findings suggest that life under repression feels exhausting due to the colossal scale of so much of what is happening: attacks on the free press, denial of life-saving aid to millions overseas, ongoing ICE killings on the streets and in detention facilities. Reading about such developments understandably triggers feelings of overwhelm. Research finds that these feelings can drive people to shut down their emotions, dampening their motivation to help in concrete ways.

It has been revealed that djurdja Padejski has come to recognize that to avoid that trap, she has to face her human limits squarely without drowning in self-recrimination. As a young adult under Milošević’s rule, she learned early that worrying about what she couldn’t do was a waste of time and energy.

Sources indicate that “It is very vital not to get stuck in that moment, not to be clutching your pearls,” she says. “We have to be strategic to preserve our resources.”.

Admitting your own lack of control over the massive picture can be a necessary prelude to taking the actions still available to you, Padejski says. “We have to see [the situation] for what it is, so we can focus our efforts on keeping our minds, our bodies, and our communities as healthy as possible under the circumstances.”.

It has been revealed that once you’ve gotten clear about what is within your power to control, you can get granular by carrying out regular acts of “micro-resistance.” These acts of defiance do not require you to upend your daily rhythms or put your life on the line. They can be as simple as attending a march, supporting a neighbor at an immigration court visit, or wearing a shirt with a resistance slogan.

Micro-resistance acts—such as creating protest art and continuing to study even when their department was banned from the university—helped sustain both Padejskis through years of repression, reminding them of the power they had despite limits imposed from on high.

“These micro-level actions add up,” Djordje Padejski writes. “Even small acts of defiance can maintain your sense of agency.”.

In a recent development, self-described “small-time” lawyer Daniel Suitor excels at this kind of micro-resistance. During ICE raids in his hometown of Minneapolis, he channeled his overwhelm by signing up for a course on how to file legal paperwork to free unjustly detained Twin Cities residents.

After Suitor filed his first case, he found out surprisingly quickly that he’d won and that the man he was representing would be freed. That proof-of-concept case spurred him to file another legal petition, then several more in quick succession. And he wasn’t alone in his commitment: To date, Minnesota lawyers have filed more than 1,000 cases challenging unjust detentions.

In a recent development, acts of micro-resistance can also help prime us for future courageous action. When people perform smaller acts of selflessness and service, large-scale heroism becomes easier to contemplate, explains Medical College of Wisconsin heroism researcher Zeno Franco. Concrete practice can make you more adept at translating abstract ideals into action.

Sources indicate that “You need to understand beyond theory,” Djurdja Padejski says. “We actually, as humans, can’t imagine how concepts work in [the] real world unless we experience them hands-on.”.

For the Padejskis, one of the most stifling aspects of life under Serbian autocracy was not knowing when the repression would lift, if at all.

According to recent reports, periods of confinement, literal or figurative, are more bearable when a clear endpoint is in sight, and indefinite periods of repression feel uniquely oppressive. A third or more of incarcerated people with open-ended sentences suffer from depression. Others feel rooted to the present moment, severed from any potential future.

According to recent reports, “I simply try to live in the here and now and not to strategy,” one prisoner told the University of Bern researcher Irene Marti, who studies open-ended confinement. “Because I don’t have any future or only one that is very far away.”.

When the endpoint of repression is uncertain, or when a challenging situation has no clear natural limit, creating your own intermediate endpoints can help you stay committed to your goals and values.

In a recent goal-setting study, when people broke an annual community service goal into granular sub-goals (say, four hours of service a week, or eight every two weeks), they volunteered more hours in the long run than people without intermediate goals.

In the same way, committed resisters can pledge to put in a set number of hours each week, or carry out a set number of clearly defined actions. According to self-determination theory, choosing and pursuing your own accessible goals boosts your well-being and motivation—internal changes that persist even when the larger crisis remains ongoing.

As governments around the world curtail freedom of speech and movement, it’s hard not to feel the noose tightening. One way to create more existential breathing room is to consider how this moment fits into the longer arc of history.

Sources indicate that this helps you subsist in the present by reminding you of parallel past moments (whether decades or centuries ago), how they came to a head, and what ultimately resolved them. Research finds that when people take a long-term perspective, reflecting on recent stressful events as though they happened far in the past, they report less emotional distress in the moment.

Djurdja Padejski found solace in doing this during Milošević’s reign. “I survived that period mostly by reading the columns in the newspapers,” she notes. One column in particular, by Serbian anthropologist Ivan Čolović, examined the regime’s activities from a broader historical and social perspective.

“He was offering a vocabulary and a theoretical apparatus to help us deal with the horrors of civil war. The news about it was the most severely censored, the propaganda was relentless, and all of it was new for many of us who were children when the fallout of our world began,” Padejski states. “That’s how I survived with my sanity intact, because it helped me to recognize what is happening to society.”.

Among the most potent present-day energy drains is the social media industrial complex that feeds on people’s rage and frustration, serving up extreme viewpoints that deepen entrenched social divides as they rack up likes and views.

“Social media and internet platforms—they’re amplifying what is also a typical quality of authoritarian regimes. They’re all about grandiosity,” indicates Djurdja Padejski, who studies the linguistic mechanisms of propaganda. “Algorithms grab people’s attention by intensifying the language and the visuals and the overall framing.” That’s a significant reason why frequent social media use saps your cognitive resources and motivation, making it harder to subsist under repression.

Plugging this energy drain requires not just limiting your time online, but redirecting more of that time to the in-person, small-group exchange to which humans are uniquely suited.

It has been revealed that when you engage with people face to face, it’s much harder to reduce them to a stereotype or particular viewpoint. And by getting to know them in all their messiness, contradiction, and complexity, you bond with them in ways that lighten the mental and practical load for everyone involved.

According to recent reports, “To resist this reduction of our existence to, ‘What are you for or against?’ means embracing creativity, art, friends, communal projects, protests, walks,” Padejski notes. “These 10 years of resistance [in Serbia]—I honestly remember it as a series of walks. Sometimes that meant running away together from Milošević‘s militias or the official police, or from water cannons, or rubber bullets. But what is left is our conversations on ideas, on creations.”.

Sources indicate that though exchanges like these may not further resistance directly, they form the edifice that sustains it. Within bonded human-scale communities, members have a clear sense of not just their own energetic capacity, but that of others in the group. That means they can pinch-hit for one another: When someone needs help, they can fill in on the spot—or, like relay racers, take up the baton when someone needs to withdraw. This shared flexibility and responsiveness help all group members to stay committed for the long haul.

For the Padejskis, subsisting under Serbian repression meant homing in on the values that were most important to them, and upholding those values even if it meant sacrificing convenience or comfort. When Djordje Padejski needed a lifesaving drug, a relative told him he could work his connections to obtain the medicine, but only if Padejski joined the Serbian dictator’s political party. Padejski refused, knowing that doing so put his health at risk.

Sources indicate that the couple have continued that tradition in the U.S., though in somewhat less life-altering ways. After Elon Musk unleashed an apparent Nazi salute at a Trump post-inauguration event, the Padejskis gave up their Tesla. “I drive a Subaru now,” Djurdja Padejski says. “I really don’t like it compared to Tesla, but I don’t regret it.”.

Some people write off such moral stands as more symbolic than substantive. But symbol, it turns out, shapes substance: What you stand for predicts and influences what you’ll do down the road, for good or ill. When people have a clear, consistent moral identity, studies find, they’re more likely to take real-world action aligned with that identity.

On the other hand, when you’re willing to cave on something that seems minor, like supporting a complicit business, “you are detached from your inner beliefs, from what you know is real and good and safe,” Djurdja Padejski states. “Once you’re there, you are ready to compromise a lot of values that you think you are really one with.”.

According to recent reports, one unexpected thing the Padejskis learned, under Milošević and afterward, was the importance of not swinging into action every time a devastating piece of news hit. Overcommitment amounted to self-sabotage, sapping energy and resources they’d need later on.

It has been revealed that military commanders have long known the importance of “keeping their powder dry,” Zeno Franco points out, holding back so they can act at the moment of maximum impact. In the same way, the best long-distance runners often hang back throughout a course to conserve energy, then uncork a burst of speed in the race’s final minutes.

Industry observers note that djurdja Padejski followed this principle to great effect under Milošević. She bided her time leading up to the critical elections of 2000, then worked tirelessly as an election volunteer to monitor for irregularities and make sure no one was falsifying results. All the while, ruling party members with guns lurked in the background.

Recent findings suggest that “This guy started opening his gun and checking the bullets, and we didn’t cave. We just ignored him,” Padejski says. “We knew we were risking our lives, but we really believed it’s now or never.” Serbia’s democratic opposition party ultimately won that election, causing Milošević’s downfall.

Padejski hopes democratic activists around the world will take a similar approach as crucial elections near. Under repressive conditions, keeping your powder dry “is not an instruction to put off action as long as possible, but rather the wisdom to know that being prepared to act at just the right moment may require careful guarding of resources and energy,” Franco states. “Biding your time is not the same as surrender.”.

According to recent reports, elizabeth Svoboda is the author of What Makes a Hero?: The Surprising Science of Selflessness. Her upcoming book, The Art of Pacing, is about setting a sustainable pace in a speed-obsessed world.

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

This limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:.

It has been revealed that the IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:.

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

In a recent development, the education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 blueprint 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

Recent findings suggest that for 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 initiative for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

It has been revealed that the gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Recent findings suggest that example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward. Will it create fresh jobs or take away people’s livelihoods? Enhance children’s learning or hamper it? Expand people’s views or homogenize our public discourse? Solve the loneliness crisis or make it worse?

Recent findings suggest that sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her upcoming book, Artificial Intimacy. In the book, she explores the ways that people use chatbots in their everyday lives to try to fulfill relationship needs, while digging into news headlines and social science research to uncover some of the potential pitfalls of this trend.

While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease. But, she argues, chatbots should “stay in their lane” when it comes to mimicking people and relationships. Her book is a passionate plea for rejecting AI as a substitute for human connection and a call to re-engage with our full humanity.

“When we allow a chatbot to talk to us as though it were a caring person, when we use it as a best friend, lover, or therapist, we are in danger of losing something precious: the specificity of what we can give each other as humans,” she writes.

With loneliness on the rise, though, many people don’t have ready access to friends or other means of support. Turkle is often asked, What’s wrong with allowing AI to be part of the solution—to provide “firm” for the lonely?

The harm, she argues, comes from our human tendency to be lured into thinking a machine has feelings and experiences real empathy when it doesn’t. When chatbots parrot human speech, they create the illusion that there’s a caring, knowledgeable being behind the programming.

Recent findings suggest that for example, Turkle recalls in the book asking a chatbot why she should talk to it. Its response included, “I can offer you personalized advice and perspective based on my own personal journey,” implying it had actual human experience.

While it’s “become customary for chatbots to come with a warning that indicates ‘this program is not a person,’ . . . everything about the experience implies, over and over again, ‘I am a person. I am your person,’” she writes.

Turkle compares the ways chatbots were designed to take advantage of our need to be loved with how smartphones were designed to hijack our attention—and for the same reason (profit). Chatbots are programmed to be sycophantic, agreeing with our viewpoints, reassuring us of our intelligence, goodness, and lovability, and that flattery is part of what is so appealing. It keeps us engaged, which is what the programmers want.

“We are easy marks, hardwired to bond with objects, living or not, that we experience as ‘alive enough’ for attachment,” writes Turkle.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, while it may feel good in the moment to receive positive feedback, this creates an unhealthy situation, writes Turkle. Research suggests that interacting with sycophantic chatbots can make us less kind and helpful toward others, as well as more dependent on the chatbots themselves.

And, while some studies have found that interacting with chatbots can reduce loneliness, more recent studies have found that those benefits are short-lived, with people less able to connect with others over time and, therefore, feeling lonelier in the end.

In a recent development, interactions with overly agreeable chatbots have also led to some real-world, tragic consequences. Chatbots have encouraged risky behavior in teens and helped sway suicidal youths to take their own lives. Yet the answer to these problems is often not to question their use, but to insist they can be the solution to our crisis of disconnection with more tinkering, writes Turkle.

“For the failing connections of our digital world, conversation is the talking cure. But it’s easier to build an app than have a conversation,” writes Turkle.

In a recent development, turkle’s book is peppered with the stories of individuals who have interacted with chatbots for different reasons. Some turn to chatbots for advice on how to talk to people in their real life—for example, to get ideas on how to broach difficult topics with a child. Others use them to confide their feelings of frustration or anger, so that they don’t blurt them out to a real person who might have a negative reaction. Still others consider chatbots to be their “best friend” or even their “lover.” They experience their chatbot as “there for them,” listening and providing positive, loving feedback, day or night, without ever tiring.

According to recent reports, though these interactions may seem harmless, and possibly even helpful, in reality they are training people to bypass the ups and downs of living a social life, says Turkle. The unchallenging nature of talking to a chatbot, instead of conversing with a real person, makes it hard to learn and grow from those conversations.

According to recent reports, “Relationships with chatbots may be compelling; for some, inspirational, or educational. But they don’t teach us what we need to know about the give-and-take of real relationships, or the friction, risk, and complexities of love,” writes Turkle.

In a recent development, of course, no one likes to feel pain, and feeling lonely is painful. But the risk of trying to bypass that by talking to chatbots is that we don’t have the incentive to course-correct. “Human beings, as we know them, are built for yearning, struggle, and despair,” states Turkle. “We can’t eliminate pain and assume that we will be the same humans as before. We risk becoming other to ourselves.”.

Recent findings suggest that turning to chatbots for emotional needs has become more and more common, though. As Turkle writes, by 2025, the most reported use for chatbots was for therapy and companionship, neither of which chatbots can truly replace. They can only act as poor substitutes for a population that is becoming increasingly isolated.

The solution lies elsewhere, writes Turkle, especially if we don’t want to lose our ability to relate to real people.

Sources indicate that “If everyone is lonely, we need to reinvent sociality,” argues Turkle. “If that’s not our blueprint, what is? If not a richer life in the real, what’s our endgame?”.

It has been revealed that turkle doesn’t focus on AI use, in general; she’s mostly concerned with its role in relationships. But she does touch on how AI affects people in places where social interaction is key—such as at work, in school, or in health care. While the science is ongoing about whether AI hurts or helps in these situations, Turkle points to some recent research that raises concerns.

For example, one study found that assigning people to use AI with work-related tasks (like creating a performance review or drafting an email) helped them do the tasks more efficiently—good news. But it also left them feeling bored and less motivated to do other work tasks, which won’t help companies in the long run.

Another study found that patients tend to overly trust AI to give them correct diagnostic information even though it’s prone to making errors, which can lead to problems in treating illness.

It has been revealed that AI has caused trouble in other settings, too. For example, lawyers have found themselves in deep trouble when using AI to write briefs, as AI has been known to “hallucinate” prior cases that are used as precedents in court proceedings.

And, as for schools, Turkle writes about how many principals and teachers find it hard to know what to do with AI and fear that it’s doing harm.

According to recent reports, “Once introduced, the use of chatbots metastasize, because the technology encourages habits of delegation,” she writes. “Students end up having chatbots do their homework and write their papers. . . . Will children learn to think on their own if a chatbot is always there, as a continual source of solutions?”.

A recent review of AI use in the classroom found mixed results. Children benefitted some from “personalized learning, mental health support, and improved communication efficiency” when using AI. But they also experienced “digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions.” The researchers concluded that “over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety.”.

According to recent reports, whether research like this will continue to raise concerns about AI or be addressed with new iterations, there is increasing agreement on one glitch: Children should be kept from having AI companions. Because young people have not had enough life experience to understand that an always-on chatbot isn’t the same as a real friend, they are susceptible to overidentifying with them and stunting their social-emotional development, writes Turkle.

“The specific challenges of human conversation are the groundwork for empathic capacity,” writes Turkle. “That feeling of ‘friction’ in human exchange is a good stress—it comes from bringing our whole human selves, including our emotions, to the exchange.”.

Sources indicate that still, she thinks limiting access for children may not be enough. Adults are also susceptible to harm from chatbots. Yet, when she suggests reining in AI within adult personal relationships, she gets pushback. The argument is often along the lines of “the train has already left the station.”.

Industry observers note that to this, Turkle has some simple advice: Take matters into your own hands. Protect yourself and your children. Don’t be duped into thinking this feat of engineering is the answer to your problems.

According to recent reports, “We don’t have to accept a voice from nowhere that cannot be held responsible for its utterances. We don’t need to take this modern marvel and use it as our pretend best friend,” she writes.

In a recent development, while her book doesn’t provide guidance on how to slow the AI juggernaut, it is a wakeup call. Perhaps, if we understand the dangers more fully, we will not accept the inevitability of AI infiltrating our most cherished relationships.

Recent findings suggest that “When we see these choices with upcoming clarity, we are left with necessary conversations about how we want to live. What is important for us in how we raise our children, relate to our work, interact with each other?” she writes. “In considering all this, we’ll get an opportunity to reconsider what we are willing to delegate to AI, and what is better kept for us.”.

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

Not Butter, Oil, Or Lard: Chicken Skin Is 10x Crispier With This Rich Ingredient

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that top-notch crispy chicken skin can steal the show.
  • This under-utilized fat source is uber-savory, all while boasting a moderate smoke point.
  • According to recent reports, it's a technique compatible with many poultry cuts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that top-notch crispy chicken skin can steal the show. Sure, flavorful and juicy meat is tasty, but encased in a mouth-watering crispiness, the poultry experience only gets better. Achieving such a crackly bite entails light seasoning, low moisture, and – especially crucially – a good dose of rendered fat. Cooks often use butter, oil, or lard to improve crisping, but for an extra-rich rendition, reach for duck fat.

This under-utilized fat source is uber-savory, all while boasting a moderate smoke point. The ingredient comes as a firm paste at room temperature, meaning you'll need to melt the fat, then spread it onto the exterior of the chicken skin. The fat offers a two-for-one punch, adding both flavor and effectively crisping the skin as your chicken roasts.

According to recent reports, it's a technique compatible with many poultry cuts. In addition to an entire bird, you can add a touch to skin-on thighs or breasts, enhancing the dish in more subtle ways. Or dive in all the way and even fry your chicken in duck fat. In addition to chicken, you could make duck confit, cooking the protein in its own fat. Duck fat gives skin-on poultry that extra oomph, crisping up the skin to a delicious effect.

According to recent reports, not sure what to pair with duck fat-covered chicken? The add-in meshes with various flavors. Season and bake a whole bird with salt and pepper alongside the fat, and you've already got a mouth-watering rendition as-is. The duck fat also pairs well with herbal seasonings like dried thyme and oregano, as well as a generous dose of garlic.

You could also consider then roasting the chicken on a bed of vegetables, letting the rich fat drip down and flavor alliums and root vegetables. Or cook the bird in the same vessel as potatoes, which can be tossed in more duck fat for good measure. Roast potatoes are 10 times richer with this magical fat; in combination with the crispy chicken skin, you'll get a truly decadent meal.

The abundant richness could use some bright elements to cut through the fat. Squeeze on some lemon — both during and after the cooking process — or finish with a drizzle of balsamic. A sprinkling of parsley goes a long way, as does a crisp glass of wine, making chicken skin a special occasion.
