Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick

📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why do some new skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice?
  • It has been revealed that learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body.
  • The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why do some new skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice? The difference may involve more than talent or effort. It may also depend on whether the brain is in the right condition to turn practice into lasting learning.

It has been revealed that learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body. Internal organs constantly send information to the brain through the vagus nerve, one of the nervous system's major communication pathways. Researchers at Tohoku University who study super network brain physiology have now shown in mice that stimulating this nerve after training can strengthen long term motor learning. Their findings point to a previously overlooked role for communication from the body to the brain in helping new skills persist.

The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.

The vagus nerve serves as a major information highway between the brain and the body. It carries signals from internal organs to the brain while also transmitting instructions from the brain back to those organs. Scientists can influence this pathway using vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which is already clinically approved for treating several disorders.

Earlier research has mainly explored VNS as a form of neuromodulation that changes activity in neurotransmitter systems. The new study suggests there may be another important mechanism involved: rhythmic changes in blood vessels inside the brain.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers created a small cuff electrode designed to stay attached to the left cervical vagus nerve in mice. They then tested VNS during horizontal optokinetic response (HOKR) learning, a cerebellum dependent eye movement task that teaches mice to improve their ability to follow moving visual stripes. The response is similar to the automatic eye movements a person makes while standing on a platform and watching a train move past.

The Biggest Effect Appeared After Practice.

The researchers applied VNS after each training session rather than during the learning task itself. The stimulation did not immediately improve performance while the mice were training. Instead, the benefits became apparent later.

On following days, mice that received VNS demonstrated stronger long-term learning. This pattern suggests that the stimulation may influence processes that happen after training, when the brain is consolidating what it has learned into more durable memory.

According to recent reports, "The key point is that VNS was delivered only after training," says Professor Ko Matsui. "Our findings suggest that VNS may open a hidden window of opportunity for enhanced learning by making the brain environment more receptive to long-lasting change.".

Rhythmic Changes in Brain Blood Volume.

The team next looked for changes inside the brain that might accompany the improved learning. They measured blood volume activity near the cerebellar flocculus, an area involved in HOKR learning.

Using fiber photometry, the researchers found that a single round of VNS produced a two phase vascular response. Local blood volume briefly decreased before rising after a delay. When VNS was repeated, it created rhythmic oscillations in blood volume.

Those vascular rhythms also appeared to be related to learning. Mice with larger blood volume oscillations generally revealed better learning by Day 5, suggesting that changes in the brain's vascular environment could be connected to the longer lasting effects of the stimulation.

"Our brains may be more strongly influenced by the body than we imagine," says lead author Junyu Chen. "By tuning the brain's metabolic environment, including rhythmic vascular movements, we may eventually unlock capacities that would otherwise remain latent.".

Exploring the Brain-Body Connection.

Future research will focus on refining stimulation protocols and determining more precisely how communication between the brain and body supports long term plasticity.

By studying this two way communication pathway in greater detail, scientists hope to better understand how learning becomes lasting and how that process might eventually be enhanced.

Materials provided by Tohoku University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#126331. Latest Update: What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2118 w)

Latest Update: What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.
  • Sources indicate that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie.
  • According to recent reports, but when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

Sources indicate that the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy.

According to recent reports, but when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a new name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her.

In a recent development, in another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.”.

In Josie’s world, being lifted is the newly introduced social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

According to recent reports, klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection.

Recent findings suggest that now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day-to-day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

We are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today.

According to recent reports, klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

All of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:.

Sources indicate that I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing. . . . As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended.

In a recent development, “Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”.

“It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

Prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for.

When I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a upcoming sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

It has been revealed that if Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “good-enough mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik notes, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”.

We love them because we care for them.

Beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct.

In a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance.

In a recent development, gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

It has been revealed that my not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration.

This past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child.

Sources indicate that the wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal.

It has been revealed that intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation.

According to recent reports, on the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care.

Care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love.

It is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

It is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

Industry observers note that at the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate strategy to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:.

Mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

According to recent reports, it is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human.

Through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

Liza Ruggiero, M.A. , ACC, is a leadership coach, facilitator, educator, and writer whose work draws on psychology, mindfulness, and emotional intelligence to support personal and professional growth. She is the founder of Heartwork Leadership Practice, where she helps people navigating transitions, such as emerging leaders, new parents, and career changers, develop the self-awareness and self-regard to lead from a place of purpose.

#126329. What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?

📅 07 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (698 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions.
  • Sources indicate that to investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine.
  • According to recent reports, mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions. Cannabinoids are a category of substances that includes THC, the main psychoactive ingredient in cannabis.

Sources indicate that to investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine. Before encountering the odor, the animals were given either a placebo or a synthetic cannabinoid drug.

According to recent reports, mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent. Researchers traced these anxiety related behaviors to increased activity in a small population of brain cells known as somatostatin neurons. These neurons are located in the central amygdala, an area of the brain involved in processing fear and stress.

It has been revealed that when the researchers genetically silenced the somatostatin neurons, the mice that received the cannabinoid became less likely to avoid the predator odor. The result suggested that these cells play an key role in producing the anxious response.

It has been revealed that "The results of this study could explain why a good trip can turn bad pretty promptly if people consume too much cannabis or the situation they are in turns stressful or scary," mentioned study senior author Dr. Sachin Patel, chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

Sources indicate that the study was published on Oct. 2 in Nature Communications.

Tracking the Brain During a Threat.

Sources indicate that patel and his colleagues gave mice several different doses of the synthetic cannabinoid and measured their reactions to the predator odor. The researchers recorded how much time the animals spent near the scent and whether they responded by freezing or fleeing.

At the same time, the team monitored activity inside the brain by implanting a small microscope into the mice's brain.

Researchers also studied brain tissue to determine how cannabinoids changed communication between neurons. Their experiments highlighted that the drug weakened a natural brain mechanism that normally acts as a "brake" on somatostatin neurons. With that restraint reduced, the neurons became more active.

"Higher doses of cannabinoids and environmental stress worked together to synergistically release the 'brake' on the central amygdala, which in turn drove excessive anxiety," Patel explained.

Why Cannabis and Anxiety Matter.

It has been revealed that cannabis use in the U.S. has steadily increased in recent years. At the same time, emergency department visits involving adverse effects from the drug have also risen.

In a recent development, previous studies have found an association between cannabis use and a higher long term risk of anxiety. Anxiety and mood disorders are also on the rise globally.

"Understanding how cannabis affects brain function to generate its psychoactive effects could ultimately reveal new ways to counteract negative consequences should they arise in some people," Patel said.

In a recent development, the researchers believe the findings may also have relevance beyond cannabis related side effects. Patel stated the same neurons could potentially represent a broader target for understanding or reducing anxiety.

"Suppressing the activity of somatostatin neurons in the central amygdala could represent a final pathway for reducing anxiety symptoms, not just in the context of cannabis side effects," he explained.

In a recent development, other Northwestern co-authors are Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon and Dr. Luis Rosas-Vidal.

The study is titled, "Cannabinoid Modulation of Central Amygdala Population Dynamics During Threat Investigation." It was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants MH100785 and K08 MH126166) and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation's Young Investigator Awards.

Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists may have found a fresh way to reduce harmful inflammation in the brain by targeting a receptor that can already be blocked with existing drugs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the research, published in Brain and led by Professor Nicholas Barnes at the University of Birmingham, identifies the P2X7 receptor as an vital driver of neuroinflammation.
  • The findings could eventually have implications for a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions in which inflammation is thought to play a role.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists may have found a fresh way to reduce harmful inflammation in the brain by targeting a receptor that can already be blocked with existing drugs.

Recent findings suggest that the research, published in Brain and led by Professor Nicholas Barnes at the University of Birmingham, identifies the P2X7 receptor as an vital driver of neuroinflammation. When researchers blocked this receptor, inflammation in human brain tissue was significantly reduced.

The findings could eventually have implications for a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions in which inflammation is thought to play a role. These include traumatic brain injury (TBI), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, depression, and psychosis.

Blocking a Key Driver of Brain Inflammation.

To investigate the receptor, the researchers used live cultures of human brain cells along with slices of brain tissue collected during neurosurgery. They focused on the P2X7 receptor, which helps trigger inflammatory signaling.

The team found that P2X7 receptors promote the release of cytokines, proteins that help regulate inflammatory responses. When the researchers used a specific antagonist to block the receptor, the inflammatory response in human brain tissue dropped significantly.

It has been revealed that professor Nicholas Barnes from the College of Medicine and Health at the University of Birmingham and corresponding author of the paper mentioned: "This exciting discovery marks a major step toward repurposing existing therapeutics to combat neuroinflammation at its source. The identification of this receptor could have far-reaching implications for some of the most debilitating and widespread brain disorders such as Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's and Multiple Sclerosis, or inflammation-linked psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia and depression.".

Studying the Brain's Immune Cells.

A major part of the work involved microglia, immune cells that help coordinate the brain's response to injury and inflammation.

It has been revealed that to study how these cells react to inflammatory signals, the researchers developed a method for converting a type of white blood cell into microglia. This process mirrors a cellular transformation that has recently been identified as occurring naturally in the brain during human aging.

Industry observers note that the team started with human peripheral monocytes collected from blood samples and converted them into microglia-like cells. These cells provided a way to examine how human microglia may respond to inflammatory signals.

When the researchers applied the P2X7 receptor antagonist, they were able to interfere with signals released by microglia as the cells became damaged and died.

Professor Barnes stated: "Studying human microglia has long been a major challenge: once removed from their native brain environment, they rapidly lose their defining characteristics, likely due to the absence of critical regulatory signals. Our approach involved the use of monocyte-derived microglia which provide a powerful, scalable, and virtually unlimited platform for studying human microglial biology with unprecedented precision.".

From Lab Models to Human Brain Tissue.

After identifying the response in the lab grown microglia-like cells, the researchers tested whether the same findings could be reproduced in human brain tissue obtained through neurosurgical procedures.

The successful results in human tissue strengthen the case for further investigation and could eventually lead to clinical trials in people with neurodegenerative diseases or traumatic brain injury.

Recent findings suggest that professor Barnes said: "Having identified the response in the human monocyte-derived microglia, this provided the impetus to translate these findings with human brain obtained following neurosurgical procedures. This successful translation means the next stage for this research is the development of clinical trials in patients with neurodegenerative conditions and patients with TBI where there are no effective pharmacological treatments to reduce the neuroinflammation and arising damage.".

According to recent reports, materials provided by University of Birmingham. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Breaking: Ten TV Series That Highlight the Best in Humanity: 2026

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that every year, we invite staff and regular contributors to nominate TV series for Greater Goodies, the awards we give to stories that exemplify or illustrate kindness, community, empathy, and more keys to well-being.
  • Name the last show you’ve seen that features a hero over the age of 60.
  • It has been revealed that with a star-studded lead cast, all 70 or older, we follow Sam Cooper’s (Alfred Molina) experience as he reluctantly moves into a senior living community in Upcoming Mexico after the death of his wife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that every year, we invite staff and regular contributors to nominate TV series for Greater Goodies, the awards we give to stories that exemplify or illustrate kindness, community, empathy, and more keys to well-being. Here’s what we came up with this year: The Boroughs, Death by Lightning, Envidiosa, The Hawk, Heated Rivalry, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, Lucky, Murderbot, Pluribus, and Shrinking.

Name the last show you’ve seen that features a hero over the age of 60. Drawing a blank? It’s not your fault—the media’s modus operandi is to equate heroism with youthfulness. Netflix’s The Boroughs flips this stereotype on its head.

It has been revealed that with a star-studded lead cast, all 70 or older, we follow Sam Cooper’s (Alfred Molina) experience as he reluctantly moves into a senior living community in Upcoming Mexico after the death of his wife. But a series of strange events suggests that this is no ordinary retirement community.

Industry observers note that as Sam navigates grief, new friendships, and a new identity, he joins forces with his neighbors to solve and resolve the community mystery. Overcoming obstacles like age discrimination and self-doubts, the group peels back the layers of the strange occurrences. At the root of the mystery is a societal fear of aging.

The show highlights what researcher Margie Lachman calls “crystallized intelligence”: the culmination of life experience, memory, and know-how. In The Boroughs, that turns out to be just as heroic as super human strength or the ability to fly. — Shanna B. Tiayon.

History has already told us how Death by Lightning ends: Charles Guiteau will assassinate President James Garfield in 1881. But why? That’s one of the questions explored by the series, and it finds motivation in a sense of purpose–how purpose forms and how people come to cross-purposes.

Garfield (Michael Shannon) is principled and drawn reluctantly into a presidential contest he entered to nominate someone else. Guiteau (Matthew Macfadyen), meanwhile, is disturbingly sympathetic: charming, articulate, and desperate to do something meaningful with his life. Despite failed ventures, including a stint at the Oneida free-love commune, he remains convinced greatness awaits him. Believing his campaigning secured Garfield’s victory, he expects a government position to confirm his worth.

As their stories converge, Garfield finds purpose in his presidency: fighting corruption while supporting education and equal opportunity. Guiteau pursues a reward he feels he deserves, an entitlement that leads to tragedy.

In these ways, Garfield and Guiteau offer sharply contrasting answers to what makes a life meaningful, and watching their stories unfold side by side, we see how differently the desire to matter can play out.

It has been revealed that who you really ought to be watching closely is Garfield’s Vice President, Chester A. Arthur (Nick Offerman). A comfortable beneficiary of the political machine, he becomes an unlikely source of hope as the story goes on. Offerman makes him funny, flawed, and increasingly affecting as the demands of office begin to collide with old loyalties.

In a political landscape that can leave us cynical–in both the 19th century and the 21st–the series makes room for something more hopeful: the possibility that even an unlikely person can rise to the occasion, if they know why they need to rise. – Aurelia Santos.

When almost-40-year-old Vicky (Griselda Siciliani) breaks up with her long-term boyfriend, she is driven to embark upon a journey of self-discovery.

At first, Vicky is just looking for a replacement for her boyfriend—but the problem is that her compulsive comparisons with other women sabotage attempts to connect with other people. (Indeed, the name of this Argentinian show, Envidiosa, means “envious.”) Vicky is self-absorbed and yet at the same time she doesn’t have a strong sense of her own self.

We see this vividly in her hilarious sessions with her therapist. When, for example, she goes on an envious rant about a friend’s milestone, she is forced to confront the quiet, uncomfortable realization that she never once asked how her friend actually felt. In short, Vicky is not a polished role model—and over the course of four seasons, we see her empathy grow through the painful process of unlearning self-centeredness.

Personally, I see Envidiosa as an opportunity to question how we show up for others’ joys and struggles, and I take it as an invitation to reflect: How can I empathize with the ups and downs of those around me? Envidiosa is a funny and at times embarrassingly relatable story about trying to become a more empathic human being and friend. — Criss Cuervo.

In The Hawk, washed-up professional golfer Lonnie “The Hawk” Hawkins (Will Ferrell) has made a miracle comeback into the PGA tour—this time around, facing a tough competitor in his son, Lance (Jimmy Tatro).

Recent findings suggest that it’s a screwball comedy, full of dirty jokes and a rapid-fire rapport between Lonnie and his not-quite-ex-wife, Stacy (Molly Shannon). A makeshift-caddy he “picked up at Walmart” (while chatting up the parking lot, from his camper van) adds to the fun, serving up an unlikely duo that seem happy just to be alive.

It has been revealed that even when he’s pretty down and out, Lonnie is looking on the bright side of things. Everything is done with gusto—he chats up the golf ball before each swing, he devours plates of Buffalo Wild Wings, he plays mini golf with his son and makes it a full-on competition.

Industry observers note that “Son, never play golf angry,” he tells Lance. For Lonnie, life is all about golf—and golf is all about fun. Why spend all your time on something if you aren’t doing it for the joy of it?

Recent findings suggest that I especially love Lonnie’s adoration for his estranged wife, a firecracker in her own right. In episode four, when the Hawk crashes his son’s engagement party–yes, you read that right–and then attempts a getaway with his caddie in the van, Stacy hurls the cake at them, along with a string of expletives.

It doesn’t even faze him. “You gotta love the passion!” Lonnie gushes. “That is one hot tamale!” — Hope Reese.

Heated Rivalry follows stick-crossed lovers Shane and Ilya as they figure out how to be intimate within the highly competitive, homophobic environment of professional hockey.

Sources indicate that at first, Shane and Ilya swap fluids more readily than emotions. But over the course of six episodes, the two learn to love across gaps in culture, language, and experience. In one pivotal scene, Shane invites Ilya to speak vulnerably about family dynamics in Ilya’s native Russian—despite not understanding a word of it.

It has been revealed that that works because Shane does not focus attention on himself. Instead, he stays present on the phone, serving as a witness to Ilya’s visceral emotions. Their connection lies in felt care, in hearing the texture of another’s heartbreak.

In similar fashion, Ilya grounds Shane in stressful encounters. He supports Shane through panic without wallowing in his lover’s fear and entices Shane to relish pleasures outside of straight standards. As a couple, they help each other explore complex parts of themselves. We see a similar process unfold in another couple in the show, as they learn to respect each other’s different needs.

According to recent reports, people might tune into Heated Rivalry for locker room towel drops and HBO’s glossy cinematography. They should stay to see a couple learn to love each other’s differences. The show exemplifies how bridging differences, at its best, means supporting others to more fully encounter themselves, and how in the process our relationships can grow.

With plenty of additional homoerotic stick-and-ball games to pull on from the novels of Rachel Reid, the next season of Heated Rivalry is expected to air on HBO Max and Canada’s Crave in Spring 2027. — Luke Brown.

Recent findings suggest that the monstrously successful HBO series Game of Thrones famously tossed out a lot of good-and-evil fantasy tropes to tell a morally complicated story of how power corrupts even the best people. A prequel called House of the Dragon shares that worldview.

That’s why a new prequel called A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms came as something of a surprise to fans. Unlike the other two series, this is not a story about a struggle for power. Instead, it focuses on a rather naive, not-too-bright “hedge knight” named Duncan (Peter Claffey) seeking to be hired by whatever lord will take him. Though Duncan is taller and stronger than most, he’s touchingly childlike as he tries to find his place in the merry old kingdoms of Westeros.

According to recent reports, the first two episodes are funny and charming, as Duncan acquires a squire in the form of a little bald boy going by the name Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), and fumblingly tries to enter a jousting tournament. And then Duncan finds himself on a collision course with the great and powerful of Westeros. When violence finally comes, there’s nothing casual about it. We feel the force of every blow, the tragedy of every death, and the erosion of Duncan’s innocence.

I’m giving A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms the award for integrity, but I can’t tell you why without spoiling the ending. Let’s just say that the series turns out to be the story of how one simple young man discovers what is most notable to him—and finds the courage to stick to that path even in the face of isolation, temptations, and threats. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

How do you exit a life you were born into?

That’s the question behind Lucky, starring Anya Taylor-Joy. Lucky was raised by her con-artist father and taught the “family business” from a young age—but when we meet her, she navigating internal conflict with the life she’s been told to live and the life she wants for herself.

Recent findings suggest that her desire to quit is complicated by her marriage to Cary, the son of a ruthless mob leader, who was also socialized into a life of crime. The couple blueprint one final con as their exit strategy, but it goes terribly wrong. Lucky sets out to resolve the botched plan, reconcile her marriage, and protect both her life and her father’s.

Her intelligence is put to the test as she puts the pieces together, connects the dots, and outsmarts her rivals. In the process she discovers her own virtue—and that the intelligence which made her a successful con artist can also set her free.

Through the course of the series, she realizes that she does not have to pay for the sins of her father. Having never been given the opportunity for self-determination, she makes peace in the best way she knows how and chooses a latest path. — Shanna B. Tiayon.

Recent findings suggest that the Murderbot Diaries are a series of science-fiction novellas by Martha Wells, about a genderless, robotic soldier who manages to achieve free will. Since discovery will result in deactivation and since it doesn’t like humans very much anyway, Murderbot conceals its freedom of mind and consumes a lot of human-made entertainment inside its own head, even as it externally follows every order given to it by the evil corporation that owns it. Murderbot even has a favorite TV show: the Star-Trek-like Rise and Fall of Sanctuary Moon.

As a result of this isolation, the novellas are built almost entirely around its memorable inner monologues, with a voice that is by turns snarky, vulnerable, cold-blooded, disgusted, and puzzled. One of the things that makes these books distinctive is that Murderbot is not Pinocchio—it has no wish to become a “real boy.” It doesn’t want a gender, or the same feelings and drives as people. It just wants to be itself—and to have that difference respected.

In a recent development, while the Apple TV show based on the books is not quite that original or interesting, Murderbot retains its focus on finding the balance between belonging and difference. When we meet Murderbot (Alexander Skarsgård), he’s been hired to protect a group of polyamorous hippie scientists who hail from a utopian colony that exists independently of the corporations that rule the rest of the galaxy.

They are Murderbot’s first encounter with humans not shaped by dehumanizing hyper-capitalistic values, and they observe Murderbot in a way the corporate humans cannot. Over the course of the first season, they begin to realize that there is more to Murderbot than meets the eye, and they learn to see and appreciate Murderbot on its own terms. But what’s crucial is not that they perceive the humanity in the not-human Murderbot—it’s that Murderbot sees the humanity (and the goodness) in them.

In time, it becomes an accepted part of their society, without becoming more like them. Even so, the first season concludes on a tough-minded, melancholy note, as Murderbot itself can’t quite feel like it belongs. Will it someday find a place among these crunchy idealists? Stay tuned: The second season is coming in 2027. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

Have you ever been among people but you didn’t feel part of the crowd? Like they were in on a joke that you just couldn’t get?

Welcome to Carol Sturka’s world. The science-fiction premise of Pluribus is that an alien virus transforms humanity into one big happy hive mind—everyone except Carol and 13 other people who seem to have immunity.

Industry observers note that even among those remaining individuals, though, Carol stands out as a malcontent. We sense that she’s been a fish out of water for her whole life.

According to recent reports, indeed, not every viewer will find Carol relatable or likable. When we first meet her, she’s at a bookstore event promoting her highly successful romantasy series. With her fans, she’s charming, funny, and kind. When she gets into a limo after a substantial sendoff by readers, the driver asks if she’s famous.

Industry observers note that “That depends,” Carol replies. “Are you a big fan of mindless crap?”.

In short, Carol hates herself, her work, and her readers. And as we discover, her personality is snarky, uptight, stubborn, and uncompromising. When the virus hits, it’s an apocalyptic event, but Carol doesn’t change one bit—and her traits become both a blessing and a curse. The whole world wants to be kind to her, but Carol can’t accept kindness. That drives her to fight back. And that’s what ultimately makes her the hero of the story.

In the end, Pluribus is a very Greater Good thought experiment. It takes prosociality to its limits and finds that a total togetherness, empathy, and cooperation to the exclusion of selfishness, crankiness, and boundaries is a self-destructive dystopia, not a utopia. The show seems to argue that humanity needs difficult people like Carol to survive, and so invites us to appreciate what the Carols of the world have to offer. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

According to recent reports, in Shrinking, talking and listening are the name of the game. Jimmy (Jason Segel) is a widowed psychotherapist who helps patients navigate anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and other ailments as he himself is floundering.

According to recent reports, but he’s not alone. His teenage daughter, overbearing-but-lovable neighbors, and coworker-friends (with Harrison Ford as the curmudgeonly head of the practice) are all there to help him when his life goes off the rails after his wife was killed by a drunk driver.

In its three-season run, the series is heavy-handed with its use of therapy-speak among the whole gang, whether between therapist-to-patient, therapist-to-daughter, or therapist-to-therapist. Characters “feel seen.” More times than I can count, they tell each other “I hear you.” We witness, in detail, exchanges inside the therapy office—and outside of it, in a rogue practice known as “Jimmying,” where therapy takes place at such venues as, for instance, the boxing ring.

According to recent reports, in other words, there’s a lot of “deep listening”: the practice of being present, open, and empathic with another person, in a way that goes beyond just hearing and understanding words. In his grief, Jimmy himself is not always a perfect deep listener. He tends to talk more than a typical therapist, and frequently injects himself into the discussion. Shrinking isn’t about perfection—it’s about struggling to connect and growing in the process. – Hope Reese.

#126326. Tech Report: Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health

📅 10 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (658 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health

📅 10 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Loneliness and social isolation are widespread in the United States.
  • Until recently, however, researchers had little idea how many years of good health might actually be lost to loneliness and social isolation.
  • Sources indicate that researchers at Tulane University's Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine have now attempted to put a number on that toll.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Loneliness and social isolation are widespread in the United States. According to a 2023 report, about half of U.S. adults experience loneliness, while nearly as many are socially isolated. Despite health consequences that can rival other major risk factors, both problems remain relatively overlooked as urgent public health concerns.

Until recently, however, researchers had little idea how many years of good health might actually be lost to loneliness and social isolation.

Loneliness Linked to Fewer Healthy Years.

Sources indicate that researchers at Tulane University's Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine have now attempted to put a number on that toll. Their first-of-its-kind observational study, published in Nature Communications, found that loneliness and social isolation were associated with the loss of nearly six years of life free from mental disorders such as depression and anxiety. The effects on physical health were smaller, but still significant.

"Overall, the study found that social isolation and loneliness can have a significant impact on disease-free life expectancy," said lead author Lu Qi, HCA Regents Distinguished Chair and professor in Celia Scott Weatherhead School of Public and Tropical Medicine at Tulane. "This includes both physical and mental disease.".

Although loneliness and social isolation are often treated as the same thing in everyday conversation, researchers distinguish between them. Social isolation refers to an objective lack of social connections. Loneliness, by contrast, describes a person's subjective dissatisfaction with the quality of their relationships, regardless of how many social interactions they actually have.

According to recent reports, "The findings weren't surprising to me," Qi noted. "Previous studies found that social isolation and loneliness are related to mortality, especially premature mortality, and this study provides additional evidence.".

Tracking More Than 277,000 Adults.

It has been revealed that the researchers analyzed data from 277,489 adults between the ages of 40 and 69. At the beginning of the study, none had seven major chronic conditions: diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, dementia, cancer, depression and anxiety.

Using age 50 as a reference point, the team calculated how loneliness and social isolation were associated with the number of years participants could expect to live without these diseases.

Compared with people who experienced neither loneliness nor social isolation, women experiencing both had 2.4 fewer years free from physical disease. Men experiencing both had 1.7 fewer years.

The difference was even larger for mental health. Women experiencing both loneliness and social isolation lived about 3.7 fewer years without mental disorders, while men lived approximately 5.8 fewer years free from those conditions.

According to recent reports, "This comes down to the gender differences between men and women," Qi said. "Our research found men are more susceptible to being affected by loneliness. We also know that women tend to live longer than men. There are gender advantages with certain diseases.".

Healthy Habits Help With Isolation, but Not Loneliness.

According to recent reports, the researchers also examined whether lifestyle could alter these associations. Healthier habits, including better diet, regular exercise, sufficient sleep, and not smoking, measurably reduced the loss of disease-free years associated with social isolation.

Loneliness produced a different pattern. A healthier lifestyle did not significantly reduce the additional health risks linked to feeling lonely. That distinction suggests loneliness and social isolation may require different approaches when it comes to protecting health.

The research team plans to study additional population groups in the future and use clinical trials to investigate whether loneliness and social isolation directly cause the health effects observed in the study.

Industry observers note that materials provided by Tulane University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game.
  • Election season can make the news feel unusually personal.
  • Recent findings suggest that there is even a name for this experience: election stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game. A few minutes later, you have read three election headlines, watched a clip from a debate, skimmed dozens of comments, and somehow learned that democracy, the economy, your health care, and the future of the planet may all be in danger before breakfast.

If this sounds familiar, you are not alone.

Election season can make the news feel unusually personal. The concerns on the ballot can affect our finances, health, schools, communities, and rights. At the same time, the way we now encounter political information—constantly, emotionally, and often in fragments—can leave us feeling overloaded rather than informed.

Recent findings suggest that there is even a name for this experience: election stress. The Mayo Clinic describes it as the overwhelming anxiety some people feel during an election cycle. And surveys from the American Psychological Association suggest that elections have become a significant source of stress for many Americans. In the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, for example, 72% of adults stated they were worried that the results could lead to violence, and 56% said they feared the election could mark the end of democracy in the United States.

Sources indicate that it is understandable to feel unsettled when an election seems to carry serious consequences. But anxiety is not always a problem to get rid of; in small doses, it can direct our attention toward what matters. It may motivate us to learn, vote, volunteer, have difficult conversations, or support people affected by political decisions.

The problem begins when information meant to help us engage instead keeps our nervous systems in a constant state of alarm.

Part of election stress comes from the uncertainty it elicits. We do not know who will win, what policies will change, or how the people around us will respond. Research suggests that uncertainty itself can be stressful because people naturally want to understand and predict the environment around them. When we feel unable to do that, we may feel less safe and less in control.

News can intensify that uncertainty. Negative news is often more attention-grabbing than positive news, and conflict, danger, and outrage make especially compelling headlines. That does not mean journalists are intentionally trying to harm us. Reporting on threats and problems is an essential part of journalism. But a steady diet of alarming information can shape how we feel about the world, especially when it leaves little room for context, solutions, or signs of human cooperation.

Sources indicate that this can create a difficult cycle. When people feel anxious, they often seek out more information in an effort to regain a sense of control. Yet the more election news they encounter—particularly news marked by uncertainty, conflict, and emotional intensity—the more anxious they may feel. Then they check again.

In other words, we may turn to the news to calm ourselves down, only to leave feeling more activated than before.

According to recent reports, political stress is not latest. But the way we receive political information has changed dramatically.

Industry observers note that when John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon debated on television in 1960, viewers watched in a far more contained media environment. There was no endless stream of clips, reactions, memes, push notifications, and commentary arriving at every hour of the day. People could discuss the debate afterward, but they were not also carrying the debate around in their pockets.

Today, election news can follow us almost everywhere: to the grocery store line, the waiting room, the car, the dinner table, and bed. Social media makes it easier for people to participate politically and amplify voices that were once excluded from public conversation. Those are meaningful benefits. But the same technology can make political information feel impossible to put down.

It also encourages us to consume news in small, emotionally potent pieces. A headline while brushing our teeth. A video clip while waiting for coffee. A dramatic post at a stoplight. These snippets can provoke strong feelings without giving us enough context to understand the story fully.

That matters because headlines often tell us what to feel before they tell us what happened. Pew research found that five out of eight Americans (63%) mentioned they only read news headlines rather than full news articles, specifically when scrolling through social media. When people repeatedly take in emotionally charged fragments of news, they may feel a growing sense of threat while having less detailed information to guide their judgments.

Faced with this constant emotional demand, some people keep checking the news compulsively. Others decide they have had enough and stop paying attention altogether.

Sources indicate that news avoidance can offer temporary relief. If every revision makes you tense, angry, or helpless, closing the app may feel like self-protection. In fact, a report from the American Press Institute found that a third of Americans want to disengage from news because it feels stressful and overwhelming.

Tips for managing election stress while building a better democracy.

According to recent reports, but avoiding news altogether comes with costs, especially during an election year. It can make it harder to participate in democratic life, understand problems that affect our communities, or distinguish reliable reporting from misinformation passed along by friends, influencers, or highly partisan accounts.

The goal, then, is not to consume more news or no news. It is to develop a healthier relationship with news: one that helps us stay informed without asking our nervous systems to be on call all day.

1. Choose a news source that includes solutions, not only problems. During stressful times, it can help to seek out reporting that does more than identify what is going wrong. Constructive journalism still covers serious problems, but it also provides context, examines solutions, and asks what people and communities can do next. This approach is not about pretending everything is fine. It is about giving readers a more complete picture: What is the problem? Who is affected? What is being tried? What can citizens realistically do? Solution-oriented reporting may be especially helpful during elections because it can replace helplessness with a more grounded sense of agency and hope for the future.

In a recent development, when you choose a news source, consider asking: Does this reporting leave me better informed? Does it help me understand the glitch, or does it only make me feel alarmed? Does it explain possible solutions as well as the threat?

According to recent reports, 2. Balance distressing news with inspiring media. We do not need to force ourselves to be positive about difficult realities. But we can balance the emotional weight of election coverage with media that remind us of human goodness, beauty, courage, and connection.

Research suggests that stories of kindness, moral courage, and collective care can evoke feelings such as elevation, gratitude, and hope. These emotions can broaden our view of what is possible and help us feel more connected to other people. And newly introduced research from the University of Santa Barbara suggests that these emotions can even reduce stress.

This might mean watching a short video about neighbors helping one another after a disaster, reading a profile of local organizers working across differences, listening to music that helps you settle, or returning to a film or show that leaves you feeling more hopeful about people, or nostalgic about the past.

In a recent development, think of this as building a more balanced media diet. Election news can be an important part of that diet, but it should not be the only thing we feed our minds. Just as eating one healthy meal a week does not transform our physical health, one inspiring story will not undo chronic stress. Over time, though, regularly choosing media that restore us, physically and mentally, can help cultivate resilience, hope, and perspective.

3. Create boundaries around when you check the news. Finally, consider treating news less like a snack and more like a meal.

Industry observers note that snacking on news all day can mean consuming a lot without ever feeling nourished. You absorb a headline here, an alert there, and a few comments in between—but never get enough context to make sense of what you are seeing. The result can be a lot of emotional calories and very little understanding.

In a recent development, instead, choose one or two intentional times to engage with the news. You might read a full article over breakfast, listen to a trusted news program on your commute, or set aside 15 minutes at lunch to review the day’s major stories. If you are prone to checking headlines compulsively, digital wellness strategies such as app limits or notification settings can make those boundaries easier to keep.

It may also help to avoid making late-night news “snacking” part of your bedtime routine. By the end of the day, our emotional and cognitive resources are often already depleted. A stream of alarming headlines can promptly turn into doomscrolling: the repeated consumption of negative online content that leaves us more agitated and less able to sleep.

Recent findings suggest that giving news its own place in the day does not mean becoming indifferent. It means making room to take in information carefully, in context, and with enough emotional space to respond thoughtfully.

According to recent reports, election stress is real because elections matter. Feeling concerned about the future does not mean that something is wrong with you; it may mean you are paying attention.

But paying attention does not require constant exposure to distress. We can choose reporting that informs and empowers us, balance difficult coverage with media that reminds us of human possibility, and set boundaries that give our minds a chance to rest.

According to recent reports, the aim is not emotional numbness. It is becoming the kind of informed citizen who can face difficult news, stay connected to what matters, and still have enough calm and hope left to act.

Industry observers note that sophie H. Janicke, Ph.D., is a positive media psychologist working as an associate professor at Chapman University, who investigates the role that newly introduced and traditional media play in promoting and affecting character development, self-transcendent emotions (such as elevation, gratitude, and awe), prosocial behavior, and happiness.

#126324. After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease

📅 13 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1293 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal.
  • Recent findings suggest that alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate.
  • According to recent reports, the drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FDA has approved the first drug designed to directly treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal. The treatment, called Zanvastro, represents a major advance for patients who previously had no options beyond managing their symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that alexander disease can interfere with movement, thinking, and automatic bodily functions such as breathing and heart rate. Zanvastro is the first and only approved disease-modifying treatment for the condition, meaning it targets an underlying biological process responsible for the disease rather than simply relieving its effects.

According to recent reports, the drug emerged from more than three decades of scientific research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's School of Veterinary Medicine and Waisman Center. Much of that work took place in the laboratory of Albee Messing, professor emeritus of comparative biosciences and former director of the Waisman Center, whose discoveries helped make the treatment possible. Ionis Pharmaceuticals collaborated in developing the drug.

According to recent reports, clinical trials offered encouraging results. Patients receiving Zanvastro generally experienced stabilization of their motor function, and some highlighted improvements in their ability to move.

"This is a wonderful and long-awaited day for the Alexander disease community," Messing indicates.

Alexander Disease: A Rare and Devastating Brain Disorder.

In a recent development, alexander disease affects fewer than one in every million people worldwide. Although exceptionally uncommon, its consequences can be severe, with symptoms that gradually interfere with everyday activities and essential bodily functions.

People with the disorder may develop seizures, lose previously acquired developmental abilities, experience increasing difficulty walking or moving, and struggle with speaking or swallowing. Some also develop dangerously elevated pressure inside the brain.

It has been revealed that the disease does not follow a single predictable course. Symptoms may first emerge during infancy, childhood, or adulthood, and their severity and progression can differ depending on when the condition begins.

For decades, doctors could offer supportive care and treatments to ease individual symptoms, but they had no approved medication capable of targeting the disease itself.

An Unexpected Discovery Revealed the Genetic Cause.

The breakthrough can be traced to research Messing conducted with Michael Brenner, professor emeritus of neurobiology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In the late 1990s, their work identified the genetic changes responsible for Alexander disease, providing scientists with a specific biological target for developing treatments.

The discovery began with an unexpected result in laboratory mice.

Messing and Brenner had genetically engineered mice to produce unusually high amounts of a protein known as glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). This protein is normally found in astrocytes, specialized cells that help support and maintain healthy function in the brain and spinal cord.

To the researchers' surprise, the modified mice developed abnormal protein deposits throughout their brains. These deposits appeared inside astrocytes and closely resembled the distinctive abnormalities seen in people with Alexander disease.

"We had, really without intending to, created a mouse that produced these classic lesions of Alexander disease," Messing says.

The abnormal deposits, called Rosenthal fibers, are a defining characteristic of the disorder. Additional genetic studies involving people diagnosed with Alexander disease confirmed that mutations in the gene responsible for producing GFAP were the underlying cause.

"This provided an obvious and specific strategy for therapy -- the GFAP protein," Messing explains.

In a recent development, identifying the genetic cause also made diagnosing the condition much simpler. Instead of relying on invasive brain biopsies to look for characteristic tissue abnormalities, doctors could use genetic testing from a blood sample to identify the mutations associated with the disease.

Scientists Develop a Drug That Targets Harmful Protein Buildup.

Once researchers understood the role of GFAP, their next challenge was finding a way to reduce its production and prevent damaging levels of the protein from accumulating in brain cells.

Sources indicate that messing joined forces with Tracy Hagemann, an associate research professor at the Waisman Center, to create improved rodent models of Alexander disease. These models more closely reproduced important features of the disorder, giving scientists a way to investigate potential treatments before testing them in people.

The team focused on a straightforward idea: If excessive GFAP contributes to the disease, lowering the amount produced might help protect the nervous system.

In collaboration with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the researchers pursued a technology known as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs).

These treatments use short, specially designed pieces of genetic material to interfere with instructions that cells use to manufacture particular proteins. Rather than targeting every protein in a cell, an ASO can be designed to reduce production of a specific one.

For Alexander disease, that target was GFAP.

Sources indicate that the experimental treatment produced promising results in rodents, supporting the decision to move forward with human testing. A clinical trial began in the summer of 2021.

Zanvastro uses this same targeted strategy. By limiting GFAP production, the drug aims to reduce the buildup of the protein before it can cause additional damage.

In a recent development, because the treatment needs to reach the central nervous system, it is administered through an injection into the spinal canal. A trained healthcare professional gives the injection once every three months.

Clinical Trials Show Improvements in Walking and Movement.

The human trial provided evidence that lowering GFAP could offer meaningful benefits to people living with Alexander disease.

Ionis Pharmaceuticals conducted the international study across 13 clinical sites, enrolling 54 patients to evaluate the treatment's safety and effectiveness.

After receiving Zanvastro for a little more than a year, treated patients demonstrated significantly better walking speeds than patients who had not received the drug.

Industry observers note that the results also indicated that treatment could stabilize motor function, an vital outcome for a progressive disorder that can steadily undermine a person's ability to move independently. Some participants experienced improvements in motor performance.

These findings helped establish Zanvastro as the first treatment approved to modify the underlying disease process in Alexander disease, rather than focusing exclusively on symptom relief.

The FDA approval covers people with Alexander disease across the full age spectrum, from infancy through adulthood.

Recent findings suggest that zanvastro is expected to become available in the United States in the weeks following the approval. Outside the United States, access to the drug will be handled through a licensing agreement between Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Recordati, a major pharmaceutical manufacturer headquartered in Italy.

A 30-Year Scientific Journey Offers New Hope.

For Messing and his colleagues, the approval represents the culmination of more than 30 years of research, beginning with basic investigations into brain cell biology and eventually leading to a treatment for patients.

What started as an unexpected finding in genetically modified mice helped reveal the cause of an extremely rare disease, transformed how doctors diagnose it, and provided the foundation for developing a drug.

The achievement is also an example of translational research, the process of turning discoveries made in laboratories into treatments that can directly benefit patients.

Throughout that journey, individuals living with Alexander disease and their families played an essential role by supporting the research and participating in studies.

"The whole program of research would not have been possible without the support and participation from the patient and family community, to whom we will always be grateful," Messing notes.
