Latest Update: Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, october’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans.
  • In a recent development, “It’s important to be in Paris,” remarked Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October.
  • The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, october’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?

In a recent development, “It’s important to be in Paris,” remarked Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.

The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 right now stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.

On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.

Art Basel Paris has been held in the historic Grand Palais since 2024.

According to recent reports, of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).

The mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.

In a recent development, that Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.

The disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?

“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” stated Andrew Terner, a Fresh York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.

The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.

Sources indicate that but maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.

It has been revealed that moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.

Recent findings suggest that the ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.

According to recent reports, today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.

Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?

Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?

The following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” says Magnus Resch, a New York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.).

“It is vital for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”.

Sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.

In the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.

Collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.

After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Industry observers note that the most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:.

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:.

Sources indicate that the "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

In a recent development, these definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

According to recent reports, national income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Sources indicate that income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

In a recent development, the FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

It has been revealed that the financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

Recent findings suggest that what distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

In a recent development, your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Recent findings suggest that divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most key predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

In a recent development, by national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, Fresh York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

Latest Update: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but fresh research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe.
  • Recent findings suggest that for years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences.
  • In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but fresh research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Recent findings suggest that for years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

It has been revealed that "Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," noted senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD.".

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear.

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

According to recent reports, the researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger.

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an notable evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

It has been revealed that "The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters.".

Industry observers note that the ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD.

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

Sources indicate that for someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

According to recent reports, the researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too swiftly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," mentioned Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'.".

Recent findings suggest that because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a upcoming way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information.
  • However, a major fresh study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most important for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.
  • Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information. Children who read easily have frequently been assumed to be more intelligent, while those who struggle have sometimes been viewed as less capable. Another common belief is that reading difficulties arise primarily from problems interpreting the words and letters on a page.

However, a major fresh study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most important for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.

According to recent reports, dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance. The research brought together scientists from the University of Kansas, St. John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University to examine which mental skills best predict reading development and why some children encounter difficulties.

Massive Study Reveals What Really Predicts Reading Success.

To investigate these relationships, the researchers combined 50,000 correlations drawn from 137 cognitive and achievement test batteries into a single statistical model. This large-scale approach allowed them to assess the contribution of individual mental abilities to reading performance while also helping clarify why previous studies had sometimes produced conflicting conclusions.

In a recent development, the findings revealed several surprises. Visual processing revealed no meaningful relationship with reading ability across the analysis. General intelligence was associated with reading performance, but its influence was considerably smaller than some earlier research had suggested.

Instead, two less frequently discussed abilities emerged as particularly important predictors of reading success: auditory processing and comprehension-knowledge.

In a recent development, "One notable finding was that general intelligence was less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses," Hajovsky mentioned. "Broad abilities such as comprehension-knowledge and auditory processing played strong, specific roles in reading beyond general intelligence, especially for decoding and comprehension.".

Two Overlooked Skills Play a Major Role in Reading.

It has been revealed that auditory processing involves recognizing and distinguishing the individual sounds that make up spoken words. For example, a child needs to identify the separate sounds within a word to understand how those sounds correspond to written letters. This skill helps support decoding, the process of working out how written words are pronounced.

According to recent reports, comprehension-knowledge refers to the vocabulary, concepts and background information a child has accumulated through learning and everyday experiences. Having this foundation makes it easier to understand the meaning of words, sentences and longer passages.

Together, these two abilities were more reliable predictors of reading performance than any other skills examined in the study. Other cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning and mental processing speed, also contributed to reading development, although they played more supporting roles.

The results suggest that reading is not simply a reflection of overall intelligence or how effectively a child processes visual information. Instead, it depends on several interconnected abilities, with language-related skills playing especially notable roles.

What the Findings Mean for Children Who Struggle to Read.

Sources indicate that the research could help educators better understand why individual students experience reading difficulties. Rather than treating all reading problems as the same, teachers may be able to identify particular weaknesses and provide instruction that addresses those needs.

Recent findings suggest that for families, the findings also offer an encouraging message. A child who has trouble reading is not necessarily less intelligent or incapable of becoming a strong reader. Difficulties may instead reflect specific abilities that need additional development and support.

"Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," Hajovsky mentioned. "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability but often reflect one specific skill that needs strengthening within a larger system that works together.".

The findings highlight the value of helping children build essential reading skills through consistent support, both in the classroom and at home.

According to recent reports, according to Hajovsky, the most effective approach involves cooperation among schools, parents, and communities. Reading develops through a network of connected skills, and strengthening those foundations one step at a time can help children become more confident and capable readers.

#126261. The Surprising Connection Between Grief and Gratitude

The Surprising Connection Between Grief and Gratitude

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Life as I knew it quietly began to unravel on a drizzly January morning in 2022.
  • According to recent reports, I was standing at the kitchen sink in a puffer jacket, staring out at my favorite persimmon tree, now bare.
  • Now that the kids were gone, my husband Mark and I conserved energy by leaving the downstairs heat off, telling each other we couldn’t justify heating the whole house just to keep the kitchen warm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Life as I knew it quietly began to unravel on a drizzly January morning in 2022.

According to recent reports, I was standing at the kitchen sink in a puffer jacket, staring out at my favorite persimmon tree, now bare. Only weeks before, the tree had been so full of persimmons that we collected them in huge plastic garbage cans for our neighbors to take by the grocery bagful. Our Labrador-ish mutt, Buster, was fat from persimmon overconsumption.

Now that the kids were gone, my husband Mark and I conserved energy by leaving the downstairs heat off, telling each other we couldn’t justify heating the whole house just to keep the kitchen warm. We were real empty-nesters, ready to downsize.

According to recent reports, within weeks, we stripped our house of everything personal. We took down family photos, scraped butterfly stickers from hidden corners, and painted over the teal walls preteen girls had decorated. All traces of our family life vanished. We put our home on the market. It was the end of an era.

In a recent development, in December, my seemingly super-fit mom was diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Our house still hadn’t sold—by the time we put it on the market, mortgage rates had started climbing for the first time in two decades—but I moved into my childhood bedroom at my parents’ home to help my dad care for my mom. She passed away four months later.

A week before my mom’s memorial, I myself was diagnosed with invasive breast cancer. And a few days after my first cancer-related surgery, a close cousin died of an accidental overdose just after his 50th birthday.

In a recent development, also during that time, a dear college friend, a fit, athletic doctor, had a fatal heart attack. And while I was having radiation for my breast cancer, our beloved dog Buster was diagnosed with lymphoma and needed to be put down.

Other losses were expected and even positive. Our house finally sold, and so we stated goodbye to the home where we had raised our four kids. I packed up that house through tears—for my mom, for my health, for my beloved dog and cousin and college friend, sobbing as I threw away things that marked my kids’ childhoods: boxes of ribbons from horse highlights and swim meets, SAT score reports, so many old shoes and backpacks, homemade Harry Potter wands.

Mark and I put our stuff in storage and moved in with my dad for real while we renovated a newly introduced house in Berkeley. I loved this time with my dad; it made my cancer treatment and everything else bearable. He had always been my person, and now I got to cry and laugh with him every day, with no space between us.

In a recent development, about a year after my mom died, we finally moved into our new house. The first morning I woke up there and looked out the window at the whole Bay Area, I was astonished to see not one, but four rainbows touching down on the water of the San Francisco Bay. I felt welcomed and reassured that I was right where I was meant to be.

According to recent reports, but then my brother-in-law Brian was diagnosed with a malignant brain tumor, the kind that doesn’t usually respond to chemo or radiation. They did everything anyway—brain surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, experimental drugs, an electromagnetic cap, expensive immunotherapy from Germany—but less than nine months later, he too passed away. I’ve never known a man with a bigger heart than Brian; when he died, we lost the emotional center on Mark’s side of the family.

Industry observers note that our family was devastated. Again.

In a recent development, with each of these losses and life changes, I picked myself up and told my friends that at least it wasn’t my dad. When my dad dies, I’m going to stay in bed for a year, I said. When my dad dies, expect my complete collapse. I started believing that I could bear anything except for losing my father, my oldest and dearest friend. The loss of my father would leave a hole in my heart I knew I could never fill.

And then, in April of 2025, one month to the day after we lost Brian, my 84-year-old dad passed away.

He was still driving, doing Pilates, and walking his dog Annie around his hilly neighborhood. He was still sharp as a tack, still hilarious, still going out every day to meet his many friends or his brother, Jud. He still volunteered and mentored others.

One week, he was fully with us, bringing me a burrito for dinner at my nephew’s Little League game, taking us to dinner at the club where he’d been a lifelong member, buying tickets to a Giants game. The next week, he was gone.

My brother and I decided it “made sense” to sell our childhood home, a place that had anchored our extended family for nearly 50 years. But I could not make sense of how I could lose everything that centered me, my whole foundation, so fucking fast.

It has been revealed that still, I didn’t utterly collapse. I learned how to grieve in small moments throughout the day; how to keep putting one foot in front of the other while still feeling loss. I cried before and after work as I walked my dad’s sweet little Annie. I broke down at the grocery store, in restaurants, while hiking with friends, at the post office. I wept while packing up my parents’ house and while pulling apart their photo albums. I was exhausted, hollowed out.

My heart was broken, but I got out of bed every morning.

According to recent reports, I started new, truly energizing work projects and slogged through my parents’ stuff and another year of difficult firsts. The first Father’s Day without my dad, the first family birthday not celebrated at my parents’ house. As the first Thanksgiving without my dad and Brian approached, my therapist remarked that grief was often surprisingly life-enhancing. That was turning out to be true for me.

Thanksgiving has always been my favorite holiday. I usually host our big family, and I always have a lot to say at dinnertime about what I am grateful for. That year, the intimate connection between loss and gratitude had become painfully obvious to me.

Genuine gratitude—when we really pause to acknowledge how valuable something is—inherently involves recognizing the impermanence of that thing. True gratitude carries the awareness that what we’re grateful for won’t last forever; it’s here now but could be gone tomorrow. That awareness is what makes a moment feel more vivid and precious.

I think one gift of loss is that it can make us more intensely grateful. Not because we’re anxious about losing someone or something, but because we’ve learned viscerally that everything is temporary—and therefore extraordinary.

Industry observers note that this crucible of loss and gratitude burned away my tolerance for anything that didn’t feel essential, helping me return to a deep spirituality. Standing at the edge of my own mortality and watching the structures of my life dissolve one by one fundamentally reordered my sense of what matters. Grief is the price of love, and it teaches us that love is what matters most.

Sources indicate that so much loss has made pretense impossible for me. Grief strips us down and cracks us open, breaking down the defenses and distractions that keep us living on the surface. In the past few years, I’ve been to deep places, emotionally and existentially, that only truth can reach. I can’t un-know that now. Superficiality has started to feel like I’m being asked to forget the hard-won truth about how fragile and precious life actually is.

When we’re grieving, we can’t pretend. We can’t avoid our own vulnerability or the fact that everything ends. And while that’s devastating, it’s also strangely liberating. I feel more at peace, more permeable, more present, more profoundly loving, more alive to the texture of my lived experience. I’m attuned to what’s real and meaningful. I feel closer to and more in love with my friends and family than ever before. I feel things so deeply, and that depth is a kind of richness.

It has been revealed that all of this is to say that growth happens in the broken-open places in our hearts. Loss and gratitude both dissolve the boundary between ourselves and the larger human experience. When we love and when we grieve, we join an ancient river of sorrow and love that connects us to everyone who has ever loved and lost.

It has been revealed that I would never choose the losses I’ve endured. I’d give anything to have my people back, and not to have had cancer. But this is the grief-gratitude paradox: I also wouldn’t trade what grief has taught me, how deeply I feel, or who I am now because of all I’ve lost.

According to recent reports, so this Thanksgiving, I’ll be at the table again, with fewer people than I’d like but more love than I ever knew I had room for. When it’s my turn to say what I’m grateful for, I won’t need to think about it. Every single moment is a gift. It’s all temporary, and it’s all extraordinary.

It has been revealed that christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The Latest Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

#126260. Breaking: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1600 w)

Breaking: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left?
  • Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord.
  • According to recent reports, in a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left? This unusual arrangement is one of the most intriguing features of the nervous system, and scientists have proposed a latest explanation that reaches back hundreds of millions of years.

Dr. Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang specializes in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, they have examined the evolutionary origins of the brain's crossed connections.

According to recent reports, in a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). Their hypothesis suggests that these connections may have developed because evolution built new brain circuits around an ancient visual system.

The brain contains numerous pathways that cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other. Understanding why these contralateral (midline-crossing) connections exist requires examining how different sensory and movement circuits developed over evolutionary time.

How the Brain Processes Visual Information.

One possible explanation begins with the eyes. When light passes through the eye's lens, the image projected onto the retina is reversed. Objects appearing to our right are projected onto the left side of the retina, while objects on our left are projected onto the right.

It has been revealed that visual information travels along the optic nerve to a structure called the optic chiasm. Here, nerve fibers are organized so that information from the right visual field reaches the left side of the brain, while information from the left visual field is directed to the right side.

Sources indicate that some of these signals reach an ancient brain structure called the optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus). Located in the midbrain, this region helps produce fast reactions to visual events, such as suddenly noticing something moving nearby.

Each side of the optic tectum contains a representation of the opposite visual field. Deeper within the structure, information about physical sensations (somatosensory information) is also organized into corresponding maps.

Because the optic tectum exists in every vertebrate species, it is considered one of the most ancient structures in the vertebrate nervous system. Its early appearance may be especially important for understanding why so many other neural pathways cross sides.

Why Sensory Signals Cross the Brain and Spinal Cord.

The researchers also examined two major pathways responsible for transmitting sensations from the body to the brain. Both cross the center of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be widespread among tetrapods (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians).

Recent findings suggest that the first, called the dorsal column pathway, carries information about gentle touch, vibration, and the position of different body parts. Signals from the limbs and torso travel upward through the dorsal portion of the spinal cord before reaching another neuron in the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, the pathway crosses to the opposite side.

Although fish lack this pathway, scientists have identified it in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its presence across these major animal groups suggests that the arrangement emerged early in tetrapod evolution and has remained largely conserved.

Sources indicate that the second pathway, known as the spinothalamic tract, transmits sensations involving pain, itching, and certain types of touch. Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord itself.

After crossing, signals travel upward to the thalamus, a brain region located above the midbrain that plays a central role in processing sensory and movement information.

This crossed arrangement is found in birds, mammals, and reptiles. It also occurs in some cartilaginous fish, including sharks and rays, suggesting that aspects of this organization have even deeper evolutionary roots.

How the Brain Controls Movement Across the Body.

The crossed organization of the nervous system extends beyond sensation. The researchers identified three key pathways involved in controlling skeletal muscles that also connect one side of the brain with the opposite side of the spinal cord.

The first is the tectospinal pathway, which helps the body respond rapidly to information from the environment.

The optic tectum processes more than vision. It also receives information about sounds and physical sensations, organizing these signals into maps that align with its visual representation on the opposite side of the brain.

Sources indicate that imagine preparing to cross a street when you suddenly notice a car approaching from the corner of your eye. You instinctively turn toward the vehicle. The tectospinal pathway is one of the neural circuits that helps produce this rapid response. It can also coordinate similar reactions to unexpected sounds or touch.

The movement signals originate in the deepest layers of the optic tectum and travel through nerve fibers to the opposite side of the spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and certain cartilaginous fish.

Recent findings suggest that another important circuit is the rubrospinal pathway, which is thought to help animals control their limbs. It begins in a midbrain structure called the red nucleus and extends to the opposite side of the spinal cord. The pathway is especially prominent in most mammals, although it has also been identified in other tetrapods and some cartilaginous fish.

The Evolution of Fine Motor Control in Humans.

The third pathway, called the corticospinal tract, has a particularly key role in humans because it supports precise movements, including the fine control of our fingers.

Its evolutionary history is more complicated than that of the other pathways.

All vertebrates possess a telencephalon, the forward portion of the brain that accounts for much of the brain's overall size in humans. However, only mammals have a cerebral cortex organized into six distinct layers.

This six-layered cortex supports sophisticated functions such as combining sensory information with memories, coordinating movement, and processing language.

The corticospinal pathway extends from the cerebral cortex toward the spinal cord, but its function varies among animals.

In most mammals, it primarily influences sensory processing. Nerve fibers reach spinal cord regions that receive information from the body, allowing the brain to regulate incoming sensations.

It has been revealed that in primates (including humans) and certain other animals capable of highly precise movements, the pathway also reaches spinal cord regions responsible for controlling muscles. These connections make intricate actions possible, including the coordinated finger movements needed for delicate tasks.

Depending on the species, the corticospinal tract can regulate sensory information or contribute directly to movement. In either case, its fibers cross the midline of the nervous system.

Industry observers note that the researchers suggest that humans may have developed advanced fine motor abilities by adapting an older neural circuit originally involved in controlling sensory input. Rather than creating an entirely new system, evolution may have given an existing pathway an additional purpose.

A 500-Million-Year-Old Explanation for the Brain's Crossed Wiring.

Taken together, these neural pathways point toward a potentially surprising explanation for the brain's unusual organization.

It has been revealed that the researchers propose that the earliest visual circuits helped establish a pattern in which sensory and movement pathways were organized across opposite sides of the nervous system. Later circuits may have inherited this arrangement as they evolved, particularly in tetrapods.

Because every living vertebrate possesses an optic chiasm and an optic tectum organized around information from the opposite visual field, the researchers suspect that these structures were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, approximately 538 to 486 million years ago.

If correct, this would mean that the basic organization underlying the brain's crossed connections began developing more than half a billion years before modern humans appeared.

Industry observers note that the hypothesis may even be testable. Scientists could examine fossilized skulls from ancient jawless fish for anatomical evidence that might help establish whether these early animals possessed an optic chiasm and optic tectum.

An Evolutionary Inheritance Rather Than an Advantage?

The broader idea challenges the assumption that every unusual biological feature must have evolved because it provided a direct survival benefit.

Evolution often modifies structures that already exist instead of developing completely latest systems. Once the ancient visual pathways established a crossed organization, that arrangement may have influenced how additional sensory and motor circuits developed.

In particular, the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have provided a structural foundation that later pathways followed.

Under this hypothesis, the brain's crossed connections did not necessarily arise because controlling the opposite side of the body was inherently more effective. Instead, they may reflect the lasting influence of an ancient arrangement that evolution repeatedly reused.

The result could be one of the most enduring examples of how the nervous system preserves its evolutionary history. The strange relationship between the brain's two hemispheres and the opposite sides of the body may ultimately trace back to the visual systems of animals that lived more than 500 million years ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

Recent findings suggest that the philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

It has been revealed that for Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

According to recent reports, the Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and presently serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago.

Sources indicate that the current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are latest to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely new collection,” Grynsztejn indicates, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”.

The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

Recent findings suggest that during her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she notes. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”.

Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue.
  • Sources indicate that published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders.
  • What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue. New research from Florida International University (FIU) has found that several types of sleep disorders are associated with physical changes in brain regions responsible for attention, motivation, and decision-making. These findings suggest that disrupted sleep may be connected to important differences in the brain's structure.

Sources indicate that published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders. The discoveries could eventually help scientists identify sleep problems earlier and develop treatments tailored to the specific brain systems involved.

What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders.

According to recent reports, an estimated 50 million to 70 million Americans experience sleep disorders, making them a major public health concern. To investigate their effects on the brain, scientists at FIU's Center for Children and Families combined and analyzed findings from 57 studies that used brain imaging to examine adults.

Recent findings suggest that rather than focusing on a single condition, the researchers compared several sleep disorders to determine whether they were associated with similar changes in brain structure. This approach, which is still relatively uncommon in sleep research, also allowed the team to identify differences specific to certain disorders.

The analysis focused on two broad groups. The first, known as dyssomnias, includes insomnia and sleep apnea, conditions that interfere with falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting sufficient restorative sleep. The second group, called parasomnias, includes sleepwalking, nightmare disorder, and sleep terrors. These conditions involve unusual events or behaviors that interrupt normal sleep cycles.

Industry observers note that "As more people recognize how crucial sleep is, there's growing urgency to understand what's happening in the brain," stated Matthew Sutherland, a cognitive neuroscientist at FIU and senior author of the study. "By bringing together results from many studies, this research gives us a clearer picture of how sleep disorders affect brain structure and function and where we need to focus next.".

Sleep Disorders Share Changes in a Critical Brain Region.

One of the most striking findings was that both groups of sleep disorders were associated with reductions in the thalamus, a structure deep within the brain that plays a central role in processing information, sustaining attention, and supporting complex thinking.

The researchers identified changes in a specific part of the thalamus called the pulvinar. This region helps the brain direct attention toward important information and manage cognitive control, which allows people to regulate their thoughts and actions while completing tasks.

The affected areas are connected to larger brain networks that help people concentrate, make decisions, and respond to their surroundings. Differences in these systems may help explain why people with sleep disorders often experience slower reaction times, difficulty making decisions, and a greater likelihood of errors or accidents.

"Most research looks at sleep disorders one at a time," mentioned Katharine Crooks, a recent FIU cognitive neuroscience doctoral graduate and lead author of the study. "By looking across many studies, we found shared patterns in the brain that help explain why sleep problems can impact focus, decision-making and everyday functioning. With so many people struggling with sleep, understanding what is happening in the brain is key to finding better interventions, diagnostic tools and personalized treatments.".

Sleepwalking and Nightmares Show Additional Brain Differences.

Although the researchers discovered common structural patterns across sleep disorders, they also found differences associated specifically with parasomnias.

People with these conditions showed changes in the posterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in motivation, decision-making, and the regulation of emotions. This finding may help explain why disorders such as sleepwalking, recurring nightmares, and sleep terrors can sometimes be accompanied by difficulties with mood, behavior, or emotional control.

In contrast, the analysis did not reveal a consistent pattern of structural changes found exclusively in dyssomnias, the category that includes insomnia and sleep apnea.

Sources indicate that together, these results suggest that different forms of disrupted sleep may be associated with both shared and distinct changes in the brain. The particular regions involved may depend on the nature of the sleep disorder.

Could Brain Imaging Lead to Better Sleep Disorder Treatments?

The findings provide researchers with new clues about the relationship between sleep disorders and the brain systems that support everyday thinking and behavior.

By identifying which regions are associated with particular sleep problems, scientists hope to improve diagnostic methods and develop more personalized interventions. Future treatments could potentially aim not only to improve sleep quality but also to protect the brain networks involved in attention, decision-making, and emotional regulation.

In a recent development, however, an important question remains unanswered. The research identified associations between sleep disorders and differences in brain structure, but it did not establish whether disrupted sleep causes those differences, whether existing brain differences contribute to sleep disorders, or whether both processes occur.

To investigate this relationship further, the FIU team looks to examine individual parasomnias in greater detail, including sleepwalking and REM sleep behavior disorder.

Understanding how these conditions relate to changes in the brain could help researchers develop better ways to recognize, manage, and potentially prevent some of the cognitive and emotional difficulties associated with disrupted sleep.

In a recent development, materials provided by Florida International University. Original written by Rosanna Castro. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Industry News: Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone.
  • Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care.
  • We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure, an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

According to recent reports, at first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: Compassion unfolds within relationships.

According to recent reports, during adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

Recent findings suggest that this means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

Recent findings suggest that when educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on teaching empathy or kindness. Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Recent findings suggest that consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

The question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

Industry observers note that this perspective does not excuse harmful behavior or passivity. But it does encourage us to understand helping as a social act rather than a purely moral one.

If we want young people to act compassionately, we need environments where compassionate action is socially supported instead of socially costly.

Perhaps the most surprising finding from our study is that recognizing suffering alone did not consistently predict helping.

Sources indicate that many students understood that someone was struggling. The difference was what happened after that recognition occurred.

According to recent reports, one of the strongest predictors of compassionate action is distress tolerance, the ability to remain engaged in the presence of emotional discomfort. This matters because witnessing another person’s suffering is often uncomfortable. We may feel sadness, anxiety, uncertainty, helplessness, or fear of saying the wrong thing. Adolescents experience these emotions, too.

Imagine a teenager whose friend is crying. The challenge is not simply recognizing that the friend is upset; it’s navigating the delicate space between overidentifying with another person’s suffering and distancing oneself from it. Too much emotional absorption can lead to overwhelm and withdrawal. Too much distance can lead to disengagement. Compassion requires something different: remaining connected to another person’s experience while maintaining enough emotional balance to respond effectively.

People sometimes assume that compassion and empathy are the same thing. They are not. Empathy allows us to resonate with another person’s experience. Compassion involves channeling that awareness into a desire to alleviate suffering. Doing so requires emotional regulation. Without it, concern can become overwhelm, uncertainty, or avoidance. Instead of moving toward suffering, we move away from it.

According to recent reports, our findings suggest that compassionate action depends not only on recognizing another person’s distress, but also on the ability to stay present with that distress without becoming consumed by it. In this sense, emotional regulation is not separate from compassion; it helps make compassion possible.

Sources indicate that for parents and educators, this finding has notable practical implications. Teaching young people how to navigate difficult emotions may strengthen their capacity for compassionate action. Skills such as mindfulness, emotional awareness, reflection, and distress tolerance are not simply tools for managing stress. They may also be the very capacities that help adolescents transform caring into action by staying engaged when helping feels uncertain, vulnerable, or emotionally difficult.

Even when adolescents care and have the emotional skills to stay engaged, one additional factor matters: motivation.

According to recent reports, in our study, intrinsic prosocial motivation was one of the strongest predictors of helping. Simply put, adolescents who genuinely wanted to help others were more likely to translate concern into action.

This may sound self-evident, but it carries notable implications.

Industry observers note that adults often try to encourage helping through external incentives, praise, rewards, or behavioral expectations. While these approaches can influence behavior, our findings suggest that compassionate action is especially powerful when it emerges from internal values and genuine concern for others.

Industry observers note that young people are constantly asking themselves what kind of person they want to be. When helping becomes connected to identity, meaning, and purpose, compassionate action appears more likely to follow.

According to recent reports, this suggests that fostering compassion is about more than encouraging kind behavior. It is also about helping young people develop a sense of responsibility toward others and a meaningful connection to shared humanity.

Taken together, these findings challenge a common assumption.

According to recent reports, there is a tendency to treat moments of inaction as moments of moral failure. We see a young person remain silent, fail to intervene, or walk past another person’s suffering, and we assume we understand what happened.

Yet our research suggests that these moments are often more complicated than they appear.

Sources indicate that they unfold within social worlds shaped by belonging, friendship, identity, uncertainty, vulnerability, and the deeply human desire to remain connected to others. They are influenced by relationships, social risks, emotional capacities, and personal motivations.

What looks like indifference from a distance may sometimes reflect a struggle between compassion and the realities that make compassionate action difficult.

This perspective shifts the conversation from a question of character to a question of conditions.

Rather than asking whether adolescents are compassionate, we might ask: What conditions help compassion become action?

The encouraging message from this research is that the factors influencing compassionate action are not fixed traits.

Relationships can be strengthened.

School climates can be improved.

Emotional regulation skills can be taught.

Prosocial values can be nurtured.

According to recent reports, when we think about compassion this way, the goal becomes larger than helping young people recognize suffering. The goal is helping them develop the capacities that allow caring to become action.

Perhaps this is what adolescence reveals so clearly. The distance between caring and acting is rarely empty space. It is filled with questions about belonging, uncertainty, responsibility, and risk.

Young people are learning to navigate that space every day.

It has been revealed that our responsibility as the adults who support them is not simply to teach them to care. It is to create the relationships, communities, and opportunities that help them act on the care they already possess.

Industry observers note that tyralynn Frazier, Ph.D., MPH, is an associate research scientist at Emory University’s Center for Contemplative Science and Compassion-Based Ethics. She leads international research in partnership with local collaborators, examining how social, emotional, and ethical (SEE) Learning and CBCT for Educators are implemented, adapted, and sustained across cultural contexts.
